Our latest findings on extensive air showers and cosmic ray anisotropies are being shared with the community. This research builds upon previous work and incorporates new data recorded by the Pierre Auger Observatory during 5 years of operations at energies exceeding 4 EeV, complemented by existing information collected over 18 years. Together, the data sets span from 4 EeV to almost 100 EeV in energy. After reconstructing the surfaces of high-energy extensive air showers using state-of-the-art radio and ultrahigh-energy particle detection methods, we identified cosmic ray anisotropies in right ascension and declination. By comparing the anisotropies recorded with the radio detector and the PMTs, we found comparable patterns and amplitudes, except for an observed enhancement of anisotropies above 8 EeV with the radio detector. This may indicate the introduction of an energy-dependent bias due to the efficiency of radio detection below approximately 8 EeV. In addition to searching for anisotropies associated with specific sources, such as active galaxies, we looked for the anisotropies related to nearby and far extensive air showers and found evidence of energy-dependent gradients in right ascension recorded by both the radio and PMTs, especially above 48 EeV, possibly linked to anisotropies resulting from interactions with cosmic ray particles in GZK-prevention.

Notably, this finding contradicts the widely held view that fermion fields are inherently irreversible. Additionally, we derive the time-reversal of the Dirac action, confirming that the classical field equation arises from the variational principle of the Dirac action under time-reversal. This analysis is consistent with the symmetry of the spacetime, as well as the initial and boundary conditions. Furthermore, we explore the initial value problem by combining the constraints with the evolution equation, then extracting the independent initial conditions for the field, as well as its canonical momentum, specifically showing that the right-amplitude of the fermion is the only non-vanishing initial degree of freedom when considering the constraint equations. Lastly, we discuss the physical implications of these findings. Due to the inherent complexity of the fermion, we focus on the key physical concepts, firstly revealing that the right-amplitude of the fermion is entirely determined by its initial value, then demonstrating that its canonical momentum is solely driven by its time-derivative. Most importantly, we discuss how this analysis is related to the Ginzburg-Landau superconductor model. This research aims to utilize the capabilities of Federated Learning (FL) in a medical imaging application, specifically in a multi-institutional collaborative setting. By employing FL, we aim to develop a model that can accurately detect and characterize tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes across different institutions, without necessitating the transfer of raw image data. Instead, FL enables institutions to share only aggregated update information, thereby maintaining data ownership and complying with HIPAA regulations. Through FL training, we demonstrate the ability to produce a robust, institution-independent model, even with heterogeneous datasets. Furthermore, FL's ability to adapt to diverse data sources is demonstrated by its successful application on a dataset comprised of both digitized histopathology images and high-resolution microscopic images. Results indicate that FL yields comparable detection accuracy of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes as conventional, centralized training methods, while also showcasing improved convergence speed and model robustness across different institutions. With increasing emphasis on data privacy in medical research, FL emerges as a promising approach to facilitate collaborative research while safeguarding sensitive data capabilities. Despite the potential efficiency gains, implementing self-reconfiguration in complex systems is highly complex. A new approach combines a model-free reinforcement learning algorithm with an optimal nonlinear controller to create a hybrid policy that learns in real-time to overcome the high computational demands of direct self-reconfiguration. Preliminary results demonstrate that this hybrid approach facilitates real-time reconfiguration in complex systems, outperforming model-free reinforcement learning in terms of convergence speed and efficiency. Furthermore, the hybrid policy maintains excellent similarity to the optimal nonlinear controller. A aircraft longitudinal control system was used to test and evaluate the model-free reinforcement learning algorithm. Compared to model-free reinforcement learning, the hybrid approach exhibited a 90% reduction in time and performed 95% as well as the optimal nonlinear controller. In 2010, the SiD Sensor collaboration submitted its sensor design for review by the ILC Technical Design Report committee. The sensor concept is a highly precise, electroluminescent direction-sensitive module with a small active region and a finely pitched readout fence in the farthest rear of the sensor. This unique design caters to the large solid angle and high momentum gradients expected from the ILCTDR detector at the International Linear Collider. The sensor design, though initially tailored to a specific purpose, possesses versatile features that enable its use in various experiments requiring low noise levels, high resolution, and ability to withstand harsh radiation conditions. This document explores modifications to the SiD Sensor concept to facilitate use in distinct tracking environments in future electron-phonon collisions. Two modified sensor designs were considered: one with an onboard pre-amplifier to reduce signal transmission noise and increase resistance to radiation damage, and another with a readout fence located midway through the sensor to reduce the impact of limited radiation tolerance. Both designs demonstrated acceptable levels of performance. Additionally, a characterisation of the SiD Sensor tracking efficiency and sensitivity to particle mass was carried out using Geant4 simulation software. The results showed that the sensor maintained its original-level tracking capabilities even when reduced to a signal transmission ratio as low as 10^-6. Also investigated was the effect of a significant decrease in electron momentum on the tracking efficiency and precision across the entire sensor volume. Lastly, the noise levels in the reduced-fence-height variant were assessed. This study confirmed the SiD Sensor's robustness and versatility, making it suitable for a wide range of tracking tasks in future electron-phonon collisions at the ILCTDR. Two distinct silicon detector concepts were also introduced - a direction-sensitive type and an intrinsic alignment type - that employed tracking structures based on charge carrier diffusion and internal crystal vibrations respectively. The parameter space for these detectors was defined by the detector's size, orientation, and the tilt of the [110] crystal axis. The noise level in these detectors was characterised by the magnitude of the crystal vibration and the noise level in the readout fence. The acceptance criteria for these detectors included resistance to 10^16 1MeV equivalent electrons of radiation damage, a tracking efficiency above 50%, and a track reconstruction fidelity below 10^-3. The intrinsic alignment type SiD Sensor was found to have superior directional sensitivity, while the direction-sensitive type exhibited better vibration resistance. Both detector concepts showed potential for use in electron-phonon collisions at the ILCTDR. In conclusion

A new spectroscopic survey from the APOGEE-2 project has been set up to investigate K giant stars and early A stars within the Tonantzintla 2 open cluster using high-resolution infrared spectra. Utilizing data from the APOGEE-2, we obtained 22 new members of Tonantzintla 2, specifically 13 metal-rich [M/H] > 0.0 and 9 metal-poor [M/H] < 0.0 members, through analysis of their spectra and proper motions. These members primarily reside in the central region of the cluster, except for two metal-poor stars located outside the proposed Tonantzintla 2 boundary. Further examination is required to verify the extent of the Tonantzintla 2 cluster due to contamination from field stars, especially in the north-east direction. Additionally, two early A stars were discovered, identified as potential binary systems, specifically APOGEE-2S00452783+5142199 and APOGEE-2S00454779+5142243, with estimated orbital periods of 13-45 and 20-65 days, respectively. These new discoveries for Tonantzintla 2 are likely just the beginning, as the CAPOS survey is expected to reveal many more A stars and early A stars. Finally, a new red clump star, APOGEE-2S00452229+5142354, has been characterised with an apparent semi-major axis of $-3.1 \pm 0.3$ km/s per century for our Tonantzintla 2 analysis. Additionally, this is only providing half the required information to categorise the Tonantzintla 2 motivation. The second part can be found in a different reference, however, it is predicted that a full understanding can be achieved once the entire CAPOS data is released. Nonetheless, this new spectroscopic survey has greatly expanded our knowledge and understanding of the central regions of the Tonantzintla 2 cluster despite some uncertainties. To conclude, a new spectroscopic survey from the APOGEE-2 project has greatly expanded our knowledge of the central region of the Tonantzintla 2 cluster through high-resolution infrared spectra analysis. This has allowed for the detection of 22 new members, specifically 9 metal-poor and 13 metal-rich members, mostly residing within the central region of the cluster. This new survey has significantly increased our knowledge of the Tonantzintla 2 region despite some uncertainties

A renormalization group approach offers a powerful tool for understanding complex systems far from equilibrium, including active nematics that exhibit alignment without direction without an external influence. This concept is behind the motion of certain living cells and polymer filaments. In this paper, we provide a detailed vibrancy to the renormalization group analysis of two common models of active nematics: the Beris-Edwards model and the Active Helical Nematic models. By incorporating fluctuations into these models, the renormalization group can be used to study their behavior as it relates to the Blue-Sky limit, a situation in which the fluctuations become infinite but where certain physical parameters remain finite. This allows us to explore how the Blue-Sky limit impacts the blue-sky spectrum of these models, which represents their dynamic structure factors. Through our examination, we identify the key benefits of incorporating fluctuations into these models, leading to a deeper understanding of their Blue-Sky behavior. This, in turn, holds promise for the development of new and more sophisticated algorithms to simulate these complex systems, leading to a door ajar for future investigation. Given the similarities between active nematics and other complex systems such as turbulent fluids and flocking behaviors, the methods employed here may find application in studying these phenomena as well. This makes the techniques and concepts presented in this paper suitable for educational purposes in the realm of complex systems. Finally, we speculate about the possibility of tracing the emergence of life on earth from the renewal of nematics, though this remains highly speculative at the moment. This presents an exciting area of investigation for the future. In order to further explore these ideas, we have made available a publicly-viewable Jupyter notebook that illustrates the computational aspects of our renormalization group analysis. This includes the mathematical derivations of how to transform the system to higher scales, along with numerical simulations that showcase the effects of fluctuations. Road Anomaly Detection (RAD) plays a crucial role in Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) by facilitating the identification, categorization, and analysis of road deviations from normal behavior. This research sector has garnered significant interest lately. Most existing approaches, however, focus on recognizing broader patterns of road usage rather than pinpointing localized anomalies such as accidents, road congestion, or construction sites. To address this disparity, we introduce a novel framework called ReAD, designed to detect and highlight anomalies from a broader perspective of road usage. This is achieved through two sequential processes: dynamic road segmentation and pinpointing anomalies. Initially, road areas requiring attention are precisely divided into segments through analysis of traffic flow patterns. Next, with the aid of extracted features, localized anomalies are precisely identified and highlighted. To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed framework, we conduct comprehensive tests on a publicly available dataset consisting of 20 diverse road scenes totaling 137 minutes of footage. This, in conjunction with a graphical representation of our framework's output, serves as a basis for comparison with other state-of-the-art techniques, revealing our framework to be superior in anomaly detection and road usage analysis. Recent advances in large language models have led to improved code completion capabilities, with many research efforts currently focused on enhancing this area. In contrast to natural language, programming languages have inherent, physical properties that embodiment-based methods, inspired by non-verbal cues in natural language, can leverage to boost completion performance. Our work delves into the potential of embodiment for code, with a comprehensive evaluation of its benefits and limitations. We demonstrate that embedding code artifacts, such as whitespace and line breaks, into the input of a large language model, results in significant improvements in completion accuracy and code readability. Additionally, we show that embedding file and folder structures, as well as code executed over time, holds promise for future research in generative large language models. Our findings provide insight into the role of embodiment in the embodied language of code. The code for our research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/jbarnesspain/embodiment-for-code.Embodiment in the embodied language of code holds promise, with a comprehensive evaluation showing that embedding its physical properties can lead to accurate completion predictions. We found that embedding properties like whitespace and line breaks improves completion accuracy and code readability, with potential also residing in structures like file and folder structures, as well as the chronological execution of code. This research investigates the potential of embodiment in the embodied language of code, with the code for the research available on GitHub at https://github.com/jbarnse/embodiment-for-code. The researchers found that the model was particularly effective at generating code snippets for tasks it had been trained on, but struggled when asked to create novel code. To improve performance, they experimented with different forms of embodiment, eventually finding that embedding the structure of code folders had a positive impact. However, embedding the order in which the code was modified had no benefit. The study suggests that the model is learning the causal relationships between different code variables, with the researchers planning to extend the study to other forms of embodied language. The model's performance also raised questions about its potential to replace human programmers. To address this issue, they will investigate the potential of the model to write entire programs from scratch, rather than just code snippets. Furthermore, the researchers will look into its ability to understand and modify existing code, with a view to using the model to explain why certain programs may crash or not work as expected. The study also touched on issues of trust, with the researchers planning to develop methods to pinpoint which parts of the model have made a prediction, in order to build user confidence in its abilities

We analyzed a dataset consisting of 1,822 galaxies from the CANDELS project to study the relationship between a galaxy's mass and its dark matter halo. Our analysis considered three distinct galaxy morphologies: those with elongated shapes, those with irregular shapes, and those with rounded shapes. By tracking the star formation rates and sizes of these galaxies over time, we categorized them based on their development stages. Our results revealed that the mass of stars within galaxies is directly proportional to the mass of their dark matter halos, with the proportionality constant varying by galaxy morphology. Specifically, elliptical galaxies produce more stars relative to their halos compared to circular galaxies, especially during the late development stages. This difference in star production behavior could be attributed to the unique properties of the galaxies, such as their central densities, which affect how they interact with their surrounding environments and the hot gas within them, ultimately shaping their evolution. Our analysis also showed that the diverse star production behaviors among the galaxies are contingent upon the mass of their central black holes. Massively black-holed galaxies tend to follow the established trend of reduced star production in ellipticals, while less massive black-holed galaxies exhibit unusually high rates of star production in ellipticals, potentially due to their consumption of their surroundings by the black hole, leading to explosive star production. Our analysis laid the groundwork for further investigation into the role of galaxy morphology in the relationship between a galaxy's mass and its dark matter halo, as well as the diverse processes driving star production throughout this relationship. By incorporating existing simulation data, we identified areas for further improvement in the galaxy evolution models. Our study discovered evidence of a previously recognized, yet unexplored relationship between a galaxy's mass, its dark matter halo, and its development stage, which could be utilized to create more accurate models for a galaxy's development. Our analysis provided a useful basis for further investigation using upcoming datasets, such as the James Webb Space Telescope, to study the diverse, development-stage-dependent behavior of star production. Moreover, our study highlighted the significance of incorporating development-stage information in analyses of a galaxy's development to uncover its underlying processes. Our results also showed that the diverse, development-stage-dependent behavior of star production, as observed in our dataset, is consistent across nearby galaxies, as observed in a separate study. Our analysis also touched on the relationship between a galaxy's development stage, its color, and its star production rate, as observed in a separate study, as well as provided evidence for new, interesting patterns in this relationship. While aerosol impact on solar radiation is well understood, determining aerosol optical depth (AOD) remains challenging due to variability in sun spectral brightness. In this research, we present two new approaches for AOD estimation based on solar radiation measurements: the first relies on inverse problems and Bayesian inference, using a Bayesian Monte Carlo method; the second, a traditional frequency domain analysis. Findings indicate that the first method yields accurate results for AOD across different wavelengths. In contrast, the second method performs well in low to moderate aerosol conditions but becomes less accurate in high aerosol situations. Our study demonstrates that combining sun spectral brightness measurements at multiple wavelengths facilitates precise estimation of aerosol phase angle and aerosol subtype. However, this accuracy is contingent on using an appropriate model for bayesian inference. When using an inappropriate model, both of our methods generate inaccurate results. Moreover, we observed that the novel approaches present alternatives to conventional ground-based AOD measurement techniques, such as filter radiometry. Our study compares these solutions to integrative AOD measurements that combine solar and lunar radiation measurements, showing consistent results. Ultimately, we advocate for using these new approaches as supplementary methods for a comprehensive ground-based AOD measurement campaign. Additionally, we provide open-access python codes for reproducing our research results. These codes incorporate relevant functions for solar radiation data processing, along with bayesian inference and frequency domain analysis methods. Furthermore, we include functions for retrieving aerosol optical properties and phase angle from sun spectral brightness measurements. Lastly, we provide a function for validating our results using bayesian inference, as well as for comparing our approach to integral AOD measurements. Our code is compatible with python version 3.8 and later, and can be accessed at https://github.com/JulianMunozA/AerosolEstimationStellarPhotometry. To better understand this process, we compared predictions from two different models - photoevaporation and MHD disk breeze - with existing and future observational data of the TW Hydrae system. Both models were run with an accurate representation of the system's properties and observed a significant decrease in gas emissions at around 10-20 years after the onset of photoevaporation. A novel approach to voicing classification and pitch tracking is introduced, relying solely on speech acoustic features that require no pre-labeled data. Voicing classification is achieved through the Kalman filter's innovation residual metric, which distinguishes voiced from unvoiced segments. To enhance stability, a modified version integrating forward and backward predictions is applied. To supplement voicing classification, an unsupervised pitch tracking method based on the autocorrelation function is developed. Strategic combinations of these metrics via soft voting are used to optimize voicing classification performance. Extensive experiments on the KWS18 dataset demonstrate that this unified system outperforms state-of-the-art voicing classification and pitch detection methods. Code is available at https://github.com/fauzilab/VoicingClassificationPBSI. Experimental evidence indicates that the proposed approach is resistant to pre-echoes and post-echoes interference. Details on the Kalman filter configuration and metric normalization are provided. Moreover, an analytical method based on the zero-crossing rate is used to verify the results and rule out spurious activity. Version 2.0 of the paper includes an improved Kalman filter metric, streamlined text, and code refresh (https://github.com/fauzilab/Voicing-Classification-Pitch-Detection). Several minor points have been clarified.

This paper presents a novel method, dynamically weighted inertial forward-backward (DWIFOB), aimed at solving monotone inclusion problems in a continuously evolving environment. Building upon the forward-backward algorithm, DWIFOB incorporates inertial components and adaptively adjusts step sizes based on past information. We demonstrate that this algorithm yields globally convergent results with minimal assumptions and efficiently handles inexact solutions to monotone operators. Furthermore, we show that our approach is well-suited for tackling variational inequality problems and share theoretical findings with similarly themed papers. Additionally, we illustrate the effectiveness of DWIFOB through its application to a quadratic optimization problem with a continuously evolving constraint. The associated MATLAB code for DWIFOB can be accessed via the author's website.

This research takes place within the framework of the non-minimal supersymmetric standard model (NMSSM), which incorporates four generations of fermions, a singlet chiral superfield, and a symmetric doublet chiral superfield. Additionally, the model includes three right-handed neutrinos with masses less than the instability mediating the singlet doublet chiral superfield. By introducing loops beyond the standard model, this study calculates Higgs boson masses, considering constraints from theoretical stability and neutrino oscillation data. It is found that considering loop corrections beyond the standard model leads to more realistic, within-range predictions for the light (heavy) NMSSM Higgs boson masses. This aligns with recent findings. Furthermore, this study confirms that future Higgs boson studies at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) and its upgrades can differentiate between the standard model and the NMSSM. In particular, the study validates the potential of Higgs boson studies at the LHC to establish whether neutrino oscillations arise from the type-I seesaw or type-II seesaw mechanism. In the near future, this study's simulations will be used to generate sensitivity reports for the LHC and its upgrades. Based on this, strategies to effectively investigate the model at the LHC and its upgrades will be recommended. It will become apparent that studies involving the standard model and its extensions, such as the NMSSM, necessitate combined analyses of particle collider, astronomical, and neutrino data to fully clarify the underlying physics governing neutrino oscillations. In particular, it will be necessary to consider the connection between the singular doublet chiral superfield and the hypothetical Z' field that mediates neutrino oscillations. Therefore, this study strongly advocates for the implementation of a comprehensive, multi-disciplinary approach to understand the underlying physics of neutrino oscillations. Research into millimeter wave technology continues to gather pace, driven by its capacity for high-speed, high-bandwidth data transmission. To address the technical limitations associated with millimeter waves, spread spectrum techniques such as OFDM are gaining attention. However, the complex, high-frequency nature of millimeter waves also presents issues of reduced coverage area and signal strength, making the topic of cell size an important area of study. In this research, we explore how to utilize hybrid transmission schemes to increase the efficiency of millimeter wave cell size expansion. By integrating remote phased arrays at both the base station and user equipment, we are able to investigate how hybrid transmission impacts signal strength and cell size. Leveraging a hybrid approach, we are able to achieve significant increases in received signal strength at the user equipment, through the use of beamforming vectors at both the base station and user equipment, we are able to maximize the signal-to-noise ratio. This research further develops the cell size expansion problem, by incorporating a multi-group broadcasting scenario, where multiple base stations transmit simultaneously on different frequency bands. To tackle this issue, we use a hybrid approach to design both base station and user equipment beamforming vectors, for both single-user and multi-user scenarios, under both singular value decomposition and hybrid precoding techniques. Experimental results show that these optimized beamforming vectors lead to significant increases in received signal strength at the user equipment, for both single-user and multi-user scenarios. A new technique for federated learning has been developed, which minimizes the need for data exchange among devices during the training process. To achieve this, the technique aggregates local models instead of parameters, eliminating the need for complex data sharing and compression. Through theoretical analysis, it has been proven that this new approach maintains the same efficiency as traditional federated learning. Furthermore, experimental results confirm its superior performance in handling communication constraints compared to existing techniques. The code for this research can be accessed via the following repository: https://github.com/djdhjdhf/FEED. The CFFD federated learning method was utilized in the study, which is based on the FedAvg algorithm. In FEED, the global server and devices engage in a \emph{exchange} process, where the server transmits aggregated local models to devices, and devices update their models based on received data. Notably, FEED requires a new computational process, known as the degree of polyaturity $\Dp$, which calculates the divergence between local and global models. The $\Dp$ metric exhibits desirable properties, such as being non-decreasing during training and resetting to 0 at convergence. Specifically, it acts as a ceiling for the relative entropy, a lower bound for the Frobenius norm, and an indicator of model skewness. The effectiveness of the FEED technique was evaluated through various experiments using different networks and data sets. For instance, using the MNIST data set and ResNet-20 network, FEED demonstrated a communication savings of up to 97.71\% while matching the test accuracy of the baseline federated learning approach. Similar results were observed in other experiments using different networks and data sets. Based on these findings, it has been concluded that FEED represents a communication-effective solution for federated learning. The research also identified areas for further improvement, such as reducing test accuracy deviations, adding more complex networks to the analysis, and exploring the generalizability of the FEED technique. Future work may also involve adapting the FEED technique to support a larger number of devices and exploring its potential applications in other domains. Additionally, it was suggested that FEED could be further developed along the lines of federated transfer learning, where models pre-trained using the $\Dp$ metric could be useful in other tasks. The feasibility of using FEED for transfer learning was demonstrated in one of the experiments, where the pre-trained model demonstrated a high degree of performance across different networks. To summarize, FEED represents an innovative approach to federated learning

This research focuses on coordinating decision-making across multiple, distributed control units within a Named Data Network-based computing system. To achieve optimal system performance, a new concept known as dynamic coordination is introduced, which allows control units to adjust their decision-making strategies over time. By applying stochastic control theory, an optimal dynamic coordination scheme is designed and analyzed, along with alternative policies for cases where closed-form solutions are impossible to obtain. Simulation results validate the significant performance gains achievable through dynamic coordination, outperforming conventional methods by up to 30% in specific scenarios. To further address implementation challenges, two practical coordination schemes are presented, one utilizing reinforcement learning and the other based on empirical performance data, both aiming to bridge theory and practice. Moreover, a comprehensive experimental framework is developed to evaluate the performance of these coordination methods. In cases where model inaccuracies or performance discrepancies occur, results show that both alternative schemes adapt and maintain optimal performance, whereas a benchmark method experiences significant degradation. To facilitate implementation, a detailed guide is provided on generating the experimental results. Furthermore, the effectiveness of these approaches is demonstrated through application examples in distributed computing and multi-access point wireless networks. In summary, this research has demonstrated the significant performance benefits of dynamic coordination over time, along with adaptable strategies for realistic scenarios where optimal solutions cannot be obtained. By presenting a range of novel approaches, this research bridges theoretical optimization problems with practical, empirical performance models, ensuring optimal results in a wide range of scenarios. By applying these methods, significant performance gains can be achieved across various systems, including distributed computing and multi-access point wireless networks. Ultimately, this research has shown dynamic coordination to be a versatile tool, capable of yielding substantial gains when implemented correctly. To facilitate replication and understanding of these findings, the paper includes detailed sections on experimental replication, implementation details, and code availability. In cases where results replication failed due to hardware limitations, additional information is provided on obtaining the results. Additionally, the paper includes a section on flawed assumptions that led to the research question, outlining potential pitfalls in scientific publication. Furthermore, results and accompanying code are freely available on a public repository, along with experimental results, implementation details, and research artifacts. By reversing the usual approach, this research has demonstrated the effectiveness of novel ideas on adaptive decision-making through a theoretical lens, by first examining empirical results and then applying theoretical optimization to outperform current methods. Automating utility function learning in multi-goal optimization problems is crucial, but current methods have significant drawbacks, including overly broad hypothesis spaces and inefficient learning processes. By initially defining a compact search space based on utility function characteristics and optimizing utility parameters through a local search, UFL-AGPO effectively learns utility functions. Experimental results on four multi-goal optimization problems with diverse utility functions reveal UFL-AGPO's superiority over existing approaches, including faster convergence, higher quality solutions, and improved robustness and generalizability. Reinforcement Learning agents can be vulnerable in certain situations, especially when an adversary manipulates key factors such as reward and action options. Since RL agents heavily rely on past experiences to make informed decisions in the present, we believe their performance V-shaped in relation to the time frame considered. Focusing on reward manipulation, our research reveals that an adversary can significantly impact an RL agent's efficiency and effectiveness by limiting its time horizon. To prevent unwanted influence, our findings suggest incorporating past experiences into the decision-making process for a more stable performance. From a security standpoint, our research highlights the significance of system administrators being aware of potential threats to RL agents, especially those with limited and extended memory capabilities. In terms of practical applications, our research has implications for game developers to protect their games from unfair cheating, as well as researchers to consider the potential risks and vulnerabilities in future RL projects. From an attack perspective, our research provides various methods for malicious actors to exploit RL agents, including through human-like tactics such as launching a surprise attack on an agent with a short memory horizon. From a defense perspective, our research explores potential ways to protect RL agents from attacks, including using special algorithms such as Experience Replay. In our research, we evaluate the effectiveness of various algorithms including Random Reward Attack and Time-based Assault. In the realm of reinforcement learning, risks associated with reward functions are often downplayed, but in scenarios involving financial transactions, national security, or energy management, accurately predicting and mitigating these risks is crucial. We introduce a novel learning framework that adapts to changing reward functions while minimizing financial losses, leading to the development of the Risk-aware Reinforcement Learning (RRL) framework. We prove that RRL allows for rapid risk assessment and achieves near-optimal return rates, even in the presence of non-stationary risks. We also demonstrate that RRL can be implemented using just two key components: a dynamic punishment system and an adaptive risk detection tool. We showcase the efficacy of our framework through simulations in two real-world scenarios, including air defense and power management, highlighting its significant practical benefits. For instance, in air defense, dynamically adjusting the likelihood of friendly fire helps minimize overall loss, while in power management, accurately estimating risks allows for optimal generator activation, thereby minimizing financial losses. We visually illustrate the results of our RRL framework, comparing its performance to existing risk-averse methods, revealing that RRL achieves the highest return rates and allows for optimal risk assessment. Conversely, risk-averse methods that assume a constant risk or a fixed number of states result in suboptimal performance. We conclude that RRL enables efficient and adaptive learning in the presence of changing risks, allowing for seamless transition between risk assessment and reward optimization. We expect our framework to elevate the field of reinforcement learning, expanding its practical applications to domains where risks are inherent to the reward functions. We make our source code available for public use.

In software development, problem tracking systems play a crucial role in managing projects and maintaining a clear historical record, with numerous organizations utilizing Jira as their primary solution. Despite the extensive use of Jira in software development, there is a notable lack of research-focused datasets centered around problem tracking. In response to this gap, this study aims to contribute to the advancement of relevant knowledge by showcasing an alternative dataset composed of publicly accessible Jira repositories. By leveraging data from 89 Jiras containing 2.7 million issues, the researchers identified 1,497 actionable problems that were analyzed alongside 1,538 artificial issues generated from problem tracking data. This research introduces a powerful tool for distributed machine learning, which leverages the capabilities of special types of aggregation functions beyond simple averages. We develop a novel class of non-linear aggregation functions, referred to as LAGF (General Form of Lagrange-type Aggregation Function), and prove their unique properties, such as uniqueness, idempotence, and consistency. Building on these properties, we demonstrate the effectiveness of LAGF-based aggregation for learning in distributed neural networks. Our experiments in the NDBC dataset demonstrate that LAGF-based aggregation outperforms traditional average-based methods in training deep neural networks, particularly when working with datasets that have noisy labels. Notably, using LAGF-based aggregation allows us to successfully train a deep neural network on the 8GB dataset, which was previously infeasible with average-based methods. These findings highlight the significant potential of LAGF-based aggregation for enabling large-scale deep learning applications in distributed environments. In recent years, AI-powered voice assistants have become an integral part of our daily lives, with their ability to understand spoken language improving over time. Current voice assistants learn from pre-recorded speech data, which may not always capture real-life diversity in speech patterns. To bridge this gap, this research paper explores the concept of on-the-fly speech enhancement using machine learning. To demonstrate the practical applications of speech enhancement, a case study is conducted in a hospital setting during the COVID-19 pandemic, where two patients are asked to breathe simultaneously in a manner detectable by microphone pickup. Analysis of their speech reveals significant degradation, including low signal levels and speech rates. To rectify this issue, a deep neural network-based system is developed to enhance speech in real-time. When tested against professionally recorded speech, this system demonstrates an improvement in speech quality. Furthermore, speech recognition results from Google's Speech API reveal a 22% reduction in errors when using the newly generated speech signals. To facilitate the adoption of speech enhancement in practical scenarios, a step-by-step guide is provided at the end of this paper. To the knowledge of the authors, this research marks the first instance of speech enhancement being applied to speech uttered by multiple living beings, simultaneously. Experimental findings suggest that speech enhancement holds tremendous promise for addressing various other real-world scenarios involving non-stationary speech patterns. We establish in this research the group structure of the platform group for iterations of bicritical rational functions, especially those of degree two or higher. Our findings extend previous work by Bell and Boussaf, who discovered a finite index subgroup of the platform group for a specific class of iterated rational functions. Additionally, our results provide a partial solution to a conjecture made by the first author. The key to our proof involves constructing a free action on a sphere, which is a product of unit disks, based on the dynamics of an icunical polynomial. The platform group for an icunical polynomial of degree $d$ turns out to be a dihedral group of order $2 (d+1)$, and the constructed free action on the sphere corresponds to a fundamental polygon with a specific type of orbit, which can be identified as the union of horocyclic circles with a particular orientation. The boundaries of these horocyclic circles are labeled according to the values of unique rational functions, which form a finite group under function equivalence. The platform group for an iteration of bicritical rational functions of degrees $e$ and $e'$ turns out to be a group with a order equal to the least common multiple of $(e+1)$ and $(e'+1)$. Our findings build on previous research by accommodating error non-normality and allowing for the number of parameters to exceed the sample size. Additionally, the analysis establishes the optimal contraction rate under an L1-loss measure, achieving the same rate as maximum likelihood estimation. Further, incorporating the L1-empirical Bayes estimator within a Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling framework yields an efficient computational method, requiring less computational expense than traditional Bayesian analyses. The empirical priors also provide a useful data-driven strategy for selecting tuning parameters in Bayesian estimation and penalized maximum likelihood estimation methods. The theoretical results are supported by numerical simulations across a variety of scenarios. The research demonstrates that empirical priors offer a practical solution for performing Bayesian analysis in high-dimensional linear regression models with non-normal errors and a large number of parameters. This research area combats the challenges posed by limited resources in newly industrialized and developing countries. This study analyzes fragmentation patterns in proton-proton and lead-lead collisions using the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider, focusing on charged-particle spectra for quark- and gluon-driven jets. Quark jets exhibit greater fragmentation than gluon jets, and this difference is more pronounced in lead-lead interactions than proton-proton collisions, suggesting quark jets are less affected by the quark-gluon plasma. Fragmentation patterns are studied in terms of the transverse momentum of the leading jet and by comparing internal fragmentation regions with external fragmentation regions. To minimize quenching effects, high-pT jets are examined in zero, non-central, and lead-lead interactions, and in both proton-proton and lead-lead collisions, jet fragmentation is closer to the leading jet's expected trajectory. However, in lead-lead interactions, this adherence to the leading jet is more pronounced, and this trend is more significant in quark jets than gluon jets, and in low-pT leads to high-pT collisions. This data is consistent with the theory that high-pT jets are less affected by the quark-gluon plasma, and quark jets are less affected than gluon jets. Additionally, this data is compared to Pythia8 simulations, which do not account for interactions with the quark-gluon plasma, and these simulations fail to replicate the observed differences between proton-proton and lead-lead interactions, particularly in terms of the dependence on the leading jet's transverse momentum. Such data is crucial in understanding how quarks and gluons interact with the quark-gluon plasma, and the observed differences between quark and gluon jets can contribute to precision measurements of quark and gluon jet fragmentation in the quark-gluon plasma. Furthermore, this data can help refine proton-lead and proton-proton interactions, and potentially reveal novel phenomena between quark and gluon jets in the quark-gluon plasma. As a result, this data is promising in understanding jet interactions within the quark-gluon plasma, and the observed quark-gluon differences can be studied in detail to further our knowledge of quark and gluon jet behavior in interactions with the quark-gluon plasma. Finally, research into high-pT jets in lead-lead interactions is ongoing, and further analysis will be based on data collected during Run 2 of the Large Hadron Collider, particularly in terms of low-pT leads to high-pT collisions and the potential discovery of new jet phenomena

We introduce a straightforward yet effective method for estimating the pose of a planar object from pixel measurements, which is usually represented as a 2D vector. Due to mild assumptions about the object's appearance, we are able to convert the nonlinear estimation issue into a completely least squares problem. This simplification enables us to utilize existing theory and algorithms for least squares estimation. Our approach has two key benefits: it usually yields a single solution and provides accurate estimation confidence. Experimental results confirm our theory that this method offers more reliable solutions compared to the established Least Squares Method. A live demo is also available online at http://comp-vision.github.io/plane_pose_from_2d_measures/. This work has been published at the IEEE CVPR 2021 Conference, where it has been accepted for publication. A video presenting the key findings can be found online at http://comp-vision.github.io/plane_pose_from_2d_measures/video/index.html.

Producing identical particles of the same sign occurs through electroweak production, often obscured by much stronger strong interactions. However, advances in collision energy and detector sensitivity allow for improved identification of this rare phenomenon. In this research, a same-sign W boson pair production study was conducted using 2016 CMS data, totaling 35.9 fb$^{-1}$ of 13 TeV proton-proton collisions. By comparing real events to those simulated from the standard model, candidate events were selected and analyzed. Additionally, strong and weak components of same-sign W boson pair production were separated and compared to simulate the effect of a new physics phenomenon. The measurement resulted in the standard model prediction that same-sign W boson pair production occurs 57.4% weakly when considering all possible scenarios. GitHub is the leading platform for software development, housing an extensive repository of repositories. Maintaining and updating these repositories efficiently is critical, as it enables developers to ensure their software remains compatible with the latest operating systems, security protocols, and performance standards. Research into this aspect of software maintenance has gained traction, specifically a new approach called meta-maintenance. This approach analyzes the maintenance activities across multiple repositories shared on GitHub to identify general patterns that can be applied to other repositories as well. Past studies have relied on small datasets consisting of similar programs developed in tandem, but this research aims to break new ground by investigating how meta-maintenance can be utilized on a diverse set of repositories hosting distinct versions of the same file. By analyzing a dataset of 1,497 repositories containing Java Aryltokennizer, this study reveals that meta-maintenance is feasible, even when dealing with unique instances of the same file. The analysis uncovers three common types of maintenance activities, and through statistical analysis, it is determined that certain repository attributes do influence the maintenance activities performed. Furthermore, specific GitHub repository maintenance activities are identified, along with corresponding commit messages, that exhibit a high degree of duplication across different repositories. Our findings indicate that meta-maintenance has considerable potential for automating software maintenance tasks, and could thus lower the burden on developers. The full dataset is available at https://github.com/abdulhkm/Meta-Maintenance/tree/main/DataSets. The Java API for meta-maintenance is available at https://github.com/abdulhkm/JavaMetaMainer. The GitHub action for meta-maintenance is available at https://github.com/abdulhkm/Meta-Maintenance.github.io. The video explaining the research is available at https://youtu.be/6_1O1LzKq4Y. The website for meta-maintenance is https://Meta-Maintenance.github.io/. General information about meta-maintenance can be found at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta-maintenance?oldid=1048555971. From a scientific viewpoint, the main contributions of this research are as follows. The first contribution involves introducing a new approach called meta-maintenance and studying its application on a diverse set of GitHub repositories. The second contribution lies in identifying common types of maintenance activities across different repositories. The third contribution involves identifying unique repository attributes that influence maintenance activities, as well as specific GitHub repository maintenance activities exhibiting a high degree of duplication across different repositories. These contributions are expected to facilitate research in software maintenance and provide practical solutions to automate software maintenance tasks.

The random singlet theory, initially proposed by Anderson, describes a phenomenon where localized spins in disordered systems interact with each other at long distances, resulting in a delocalized, entangled state. However, our study reveals that this theory doesn't fully apply to the one-dimensional Hubbard model, especially at its symmetry-breaking point. While our findings support the concept of spin delocalization, they also show that the nature of long-distance spin interactions is more complex than previously thought. Moreover, our data cannot be explained using a single parameter, scaled by Anderson's localization length, which is typical in random singlet systems. Instead, our results show that the delocalization is influenced by multiple factors including the disorder strength, electron correlations, and band filling. Additionally, our data show that the spin delocalization is not a gradual transition but is instead separated into two distinct phases by the electron correlation parameter. These results demonstrate that the critical regime between these two phases is characterized by inherent instabilities of the single-chain Kondo effect. Due to these complexities, our data cannot be accurately explained using a random singlet theory based on Anderson's model, although some aspects of our data do show similarities with this theory. Therefore, our study provides new insights into the delocalization of spin and the associated critical phenomena in disordered Hubbard chains. In inverse reinforcement learning with multiple agents, algorithms are challenged by designing a policy that multiple agents can follow, given varying observations of each other's behaviors. Our novel approach uses a hierarchical Bayesian model to analyze the agents' actions and create a shared policy, under the assumption that they share a common prior distribution. By applying Bayesian methods, our framework estimates the posterior distribution of their policies without requiring them to directly communicate. Building upon this concept, we extended an existing algorithm, SARSA-IRL, to work in partially observable environments and demonstrated the robustness of our framework through both synthetic data analysis and game simulations. Our framework's benefits were further shown in scenarios with competing agents and limited information sharing. Additionally, we proposed a method for reducing the impact of spurious local policies by applying regularized maximum likelihood estimation. Our results confirm that our framework successfully captures the shared aspects of each agent's behavior and achieves higher rewards when policies are similar. Moreover, we observed improved performance in both known and unknown environment settings. Our framework, named Hierarchical Policy Mixture, demonstrates superior performance when evaluated against eight competing algorithms. A detailed analysis and source code are available at public repositories for verification.

To overcome the challenges, we develop a multi-faceted approach where a high-level decision maker transfers control policies to lower-level agents adapting to task-specific control schemes through reinforcement learning. Our prior investigation into dark matter compact objects employed a realistic reformation approach, spanning five decades, and discovered a lack of dark matter halos less massive than $10^4$ solar masses within a specific redshift range. In this follow-up study, we build upon the previous findings by incorporating a seed mass formation theory based on primordial black holes. Utilizing a numerical compactness theorem-based black hole template, we observe a substantial rise in dark matter halo density for masses between $10^4$ solar masses and $10^7$ solar masses at a redshift of 1000. This increase is attributed to the stable existence of massive dark matter halos within this mass range. However, below $10^4$ solar masses, our model still exhibits a deficiency in dark matter halo density. Consequently, we propose that dark matter halos are present across a vast spectrum of masses, but become less dense and eventually nonexistent below a certain threshold, where they are replaced by a new phenomenon, namely, the fragmentation of supermassive dark matter holes through stellar feedback, a process we have theorized in a previous study. In light of our model's success in matching observed supermassive black hole characteristics, we suggest that stellar feedback may have played a key role in shaping the universe's supermassive dark matter hole mass distribution. Our model's predictions for dark matter halo density at various redshifts provide a foundation for further investigation of compact, dark matter-based objects. In light of our model's success, we suggest that these predictions should be examined in conjunction with future observations of the unresolved emission within the cosmic ultraviolet background. Additionally, we propose that our model should be evaluated in conjunction with the upcoming galactic center supermassive black hole monitoring initiative. In particular, we expect our model to yield valuable insights into the low-mass end of the supermassive black hole spectrum, where our model generates an unusually abundant supply of compact, dark matter-based objects, potentially leading to their accretion into larger halos. In contrast, we anticipate that our model will also yield valuable insights into the high-mass end of the supermassive black hole spectrum, where stellar feedback is thought to have fragmenting effects on the universe's supermassive dark matter holes. In this regard, we expect that our model will be especially well-suited to yielding insights based on the galactic center supermassive black hole monitoring initiative's capacity to analyze changes in the flow rates of gas and stars at the heart of Milky Way and other nearby galaxies

We establish a novel relationship between slim Sidon sequences and the nonlinearity of vectorial Boolean mappings. Specifically, we demonstrate that a vectorial Boolean function $f$ has a high nonlinearity if it is associated with a slim Sidon sequence. Furthermore, we develop an optimal upper limit for the nonlinearity of vectorial Boolean mappings with specific properties. To achieve this, we discover new families of slim Sidon sequences. We also prove that a vectorial Boolean function $f$ with certain characteristics has a high nonlinearity if it is associated with two distinct slim Sidon sequences. This result is then used to establish upper limits for the nonlinearity of certain types of vectorial Boolean functions. The findings are further substantiated by presenting a vast class of vectorial Boolean functions that achieve the upper bounds proposed. We also examine how our results can be applied to affine and semi-bent vectorial Boolean mappings. In this process, we clarify some confusing points in the existing literature and provide concrete examples to support our findings. To conclude, we introduce a method for determining a lower limit on the nonlinearity of vectorial Boolean mappings with specific properties, as well as a tool for generating slim Sidon sequences based on the characteristics of a vectorial Boolean function. We hypothesize that this method can be extended to determine a lower limit on the nonlinearity of affine vectorial Boolean mappings. As such, the presented work is a contribution to the field of finite desarguesian planes under the nonlinearity criterion. We also express our intention to make the code used to verify our results and generate the examples available under the terms of the MIT license, allowing their use for any purpose. Due to technical constraints, the source is temporarily unavailable at present but will be shared at a later date. We anticipate that it will prove useful for the investigation of vectorial Boolean mappings with slim Sidon sequences. Additionally, we envision the results and accompanying tools being employed in the development of lightweight cipher designs that take advantage of properties of vectorial Boolean mappings with slim Sidon sequences. We speculate that such cipher designs could exhibit superior performance characteristics in relevant metrics. However, a comprehensive evaluation of the proposed mappings would require a thorough review of the existing literature on lightweight cipher systems. Consequently, we plan to expand our research in this area, aiming to construct a lightweight cipher based on vectorial Boolean mappings with slim Sidon sequences that offer superior performance compared to existing solutions. We expect that the resulting work will be a significant contribution to the field of lightweight cryptography.

Quantization has emerged as a highly effective technique for reducing the computational resources and memory requirements of deep neural networks, particularly when employing binary weights. Research has shown that quantized models often achieve comparable or superior performance to their full-precision counterparts. Interestingly, the typical structural modifications made to these networks during the quantization process seem to contribute to improved accuracy, despite these changes being extraneous to the underlying problem being solved. To understand the quantization effect from an intrinsic perspective, we examined the spectral properties of Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) for binary weight neural networks and found that reducing weight amplitude (weight pruning) or variance ($k$-ary arithmetic) leads to an increase in the kernel's eigenvalues' magnitude. This results in a more stable and generalized decision boundary. We also observed that binary weight quantization further enhances generalization by inducing a more complex and diverse kernel. Additionally, our analysis explains why observing improved generalization outcomes becomes less common as the quantization level approaches its maximum possible value. To facilitate replicability, our research includes a publicly accessible code repository with the implemented methods. This research was motivated by a desire to grasp the quantization effect as an intrinsic modification of the problem being solved and has potential applications in the field of deep learning. It also offers novel insights into the Neural Tangent Kernel that weren't previously apparent, particularly in the context of binary weight neural networks. Moreover, it identifies key characteristics that contribute to generalization in these models. We identified new possibilities for enhancing generalization, such as utilizing multiple bits to represent input features, and our findings were confirmed through experiments. These findings update our understanding of the Neural Tangent Kernel by revealing that its eigenvalues' signs can vary based on the network's layer and that its magnitude depends on the weight distribution. Moreover, our research established a connection between the kernel's inductive bias and the weight variance, which modulates its generalization capabilities. In such cases, using different stabilization techniques can significantly improve the algorithms. In this study, we introduce and examine the convergence of iterative methods that utilize various stabilization techniques such as the Exponential Regularization, Tikhonov regularization, and Moebius transformation. We compare these techniques with a new approach based on the Non-Expansive Averaging algorithm and show that it converges at a faster rate. Additionally, we highlight the benefits of using this new approach in scenarios where its convergence was previously unknown. We thoroughly analyze the computational costs of all methods and demonstrate that our proposal has lower costs compared to state-of-the-art algorithms. These expressions are useful for a variety of applications, including calculating the PSF from an observed image, estimating the PSF from a raw AO image, and constructing a combined image with optimal signal-to-noise ratio. The proposed equations are then verified through comparisons with alternative methods found in the literature, and are found to yield accurate results for a range of scenarios. The PSF estimation technique is subsequently evaluated using real AO images obtained with the GeMS AO system on the Geert Bollen telescope at the Yucatan Field Station. The test images are chosen to highlight the performance of the technique under various conditions, including strong laser guide star data and no laser guide star data. The PFS estimation technique is found to perform well across these different scenarios. The research demonstrates that the PSF estimation technique can effectively account for the effects of several key factors, including tip-tilt underling PSF, AO correction, detector readout, and telescope optics, and that it does so with an acceptable level of computational complexity. The research ultimately identifies areas where future improvements to the PSF estimation technique could be made. The code used to evaluate the accuracy of the PSF estimation technique was written in Python, and is based on the PFS library developed by the research team. The PFS library was created with the goal of providing a convenient way to calculate the PSF, and to integrate this functionality into a larger range of image processing tasks. A new approach is proposed for validating numerical results of quantum calculations using the finite element method. The conventional process of verifying these results typically involves comparing them with existing theoretical values. However, the proposed method seeks to achieve this validation in quantum systems with single-particle Hamiltonians of variable hardness. The underlying principle of this approach is based on the comparison of total energies calculated classically and those derived from wavefunctions obtained through numerical solutions of the Schrödinger equation. In order to determine the accuracy of these numerical energies, we employ two different metrics: one that measures the residual error associated with the finite element discretization, and another that evaluates the error in computing total energies as a function of charge. We apply this approach to three distinct atoms: a helium-like ion with one excess positive charge and varying negative charges, and a neutral magnesium atom with varying positive charges. The total energies calculated for these atoms are compared with their corresponding theoretical values. Furthermore, we examine the rates at which numerical energies converge relative to their classical counterparts. Our approach is designed to be used as a diagnostic tool to verify the implementation of numerical methods in quantum calculations and to study the properties of multi-charged ions. This diagnostic tool is expected to be particularly useful in three-dimensional quantum calculations of atoms with many excess positive charges. Although our approach is based on the finite element method, a comparable diagnostic tool can be developed for other numerical methods of quantum calculations. Moreover, this diagnostic tool is anticipated to be effective not only in numerical calculations of total energies but also in three-dimensional quantum calculations of atoms with many excess positive charges. Lastly, this diagnostic tool is anticipated to be useful in numerical calculations of bound states. Its development and application are described in detail. In particular, we demonstrate that our approach is versatile and can be adapted to various applications. Although we present a formal description of our diagnostic tool based on the finite element method, an alternative diagnostic tool can be developed using other numerical methods of quantum calculations. Our experiments reveal that training neural networks to generate cell shapes through an implicit approach is a viable option. Our methodology, known as CoCoCo, is an alternative to previous techniques and allows for the conditional generation of cell shapes from specific input signals. CoCoCo utilizes a network that takes a point in a higher-dimensional space and outputs a signed distance function value that indicates the cell's presence. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of implicit neural representations in modeling the complex shapes of biological cells. With significant potential to improve current cell modeling techniques, CoCoCo could be utilized for various applications such as simulating cell behavior, analyzing cell development or detecting abnormalities. Two commonly used visualizations for spatial information - grid cells and Schnittke maps - are examined in this study. Although grid cells, like reinforcement learning agents, arrange points according to the Pythagorean theorem, the depictions' connection goes beyond this surface-level resemblance. Our investigation reveals that utilizing Schnittke maps in conjunction with orientation-selective units effectively captures the essence of spatial distance, whereas traditional depictions fall short in this endeavor. This analysis highlights the significance of incorporating specialized, non-linear depictions in visualizing spatial cognition. The study also demonstrates that, in a task requiring finding the center of mass, agents utilizing non-linear depictions learn faster and achieve higher success rates compared to those using linear depictions. Ultimately, the research suggests non-linear depictions are essential for accurately modeling and understanding skilled biological agents, such as humans. Conversely, the success of linear depictions in simulated agents may stem from their inherent simplicity and randomness, which could be attributed to the differences between simulated and real agents. This study examines how certain thermal noise impacts the dynamics of two-dimensional solid particles that interact through area-exclusion principles. We demonstrate that any variation in the interaction rules, as long as they adhere to these principles, results in similar noise effects. We also show that, in the absence of noise, these particles interact through a complex, reversible process known as the "calibration algorithm," which positions them according to their total polar area. Notably, when considering their full state trajectories, these systems exhibit full statistical detail balance only with a specific type of non-reversible noise mechanism. With this understanding, we apply the ideas of "universal fluctuations" to forecast how these particles would behave if they could efficiently transition between configurations through a process called "geometric rearrangement." We also explore the theoretical implications of applying this concept to real-world particle systems. We analyzed these models using specialized software tools, including VisualDSP and JFlow, to simulate their dynamics at varying levels of resolution. Our findings reveal how, as these systems reach a state of statistical equilibrium, their behavior exhibits characteristics of "universal hard-disk magnetization," prompting us to investigate the potential applications of this concept to real-world particle systems. We also considered other possible noise mechanisms, as well as expanded systems involving multiple particles, to establish fundamental principles for applying these ideas to more complex scenarios. Concurrent transmission based wireless systems, which utilize superposition coding (SPC) and scheduling, have shown enchanting performance in enhancing sum-throughput, fairness, and energy efficiency. This paper delves into the fundamentals and applications of such systems, showcasing how SPC-scheduling combinations address complexity and performance limitations in 5G and 6G wireless networks. A central question examined through this review is how to ensure reliable data detection in additive white Gaussian noise environments. Further exploration is also devoted to using machine learning and deep learning to improve the wireless performance of SPC-scheduling and deep learning-based wireless systems. A new perspective on the future of wireless communication is also offered, highlighting how AI can elevate the enchanting performance of SPC-scheduling combinations and accelerate the development of next-generation wireless networks. This Enchantment of Superposition captures the essence of this paper's investigation, demonstrating how SPC-scheduling combinations can be transformative in 5G and 6G wireless technology. A recent body of research suggests that collections of spectrogram levels hold significant promise in uncovering underlying structures of signals, potentially exceeding the scope of traditional frequency analysis. To capitalize on these collections' geometric properties, a randomized approach is required to extract relevant information about the signal, given their high dimensionality and complexity. To this end, a random matrix framework is developed and utilized to study the statistical properties of spectrogram level collections, as well as their associated geometric structures. Building on these findings, a novel signal evaluation procedure is introduced, leveraging the characterization of these collections' geometry through random matrices. In addition, a proof of concept is provided, demonstrating the efficacy of this approach in signal classification, particularly in distinguishing between amino acid and DNA sequences. Computational experiments reveal that the resulting classifier generated via the proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard datasets, underscoring the efficacy of this randomized approach in extracting salient features from spectrogram level collections. Furthermore, a theoretical analysis of the evaluator's accuracy as the number of collections increases is presented, along with a boundary estimate for the associated classification error. These results are facilitated by a novel application of the Frechet theorem in Random Matrix Theory. Furthermore, a method for reducing the bias in spectrogram level collections is developed, employing a fixed-point scheme based on the mutual coherence lemmas. To validate these findings, a set of computational experiments involving diverse signal types is designed, demonstrating that the proposed method succeeds in minimizing bias for over 90% of signal categories, with a corresponding decrease in classification error. The accompanying package includes code and data to replicate the experiments, as well as a standalone evaluator, that can be run independently of the underlying random matrix framework. As such, this research offers a flexible and theoretically grounded approach to signal evaluation, relying on random matrices and the geometry of spectrogram level collections, rather than reliance on kernels or neural networks. It is anticipated that this framework will yield novel applications across multiple domains, far exceeding the scope of signal classification examples provided. Ultimately, this research is positioned to contribute to the broader spectrogram level collections research agenda, driven by the conjecture that these collections might harbor the knowledge to create autonomous, cognition-like systems. We present a novel detection method called AUTOCOA that identifies multiple synchronized groups, as well as traveling chimeras, in spiking neural networks. Traveling chimeras are a type of oscillatory state characterized by stationary waves moving across different frequency phases. Current approaches for detecting traveling chimeras are limited to specific architectures and often rely on predefined assumptions. In contrast, AUTOCOA is a robust, flexible, and general method that works on directed and asymmetric networks without requiring any a priori knowledge. After extensively testing it on various artificial and real-world networks, we found that AUTOCOA is a reliable and efficient method for detecting traveling chimeras. Furthermore, we observed that it is capable of detecting multiple synchronized groups within the same oscillatory state. Therefore, AUTOCOA represents a valuable resource for analyzing and understanding the complex dynamics of spiking neural networks. The code is freely available at https://github.com/JulienArchereau/AUTOCOA/tree/main. Additionally, a movie showcasing our results can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.17632/3x7wcmw744/1. Determining Planetary Masses from Observations of a Multiple System, such as ALMA, SPHERE, or Gravitational Microlensing, often requires accurate calculations of how light interacts with planets under General Relativity. However, accounting for the random fluctuations inherent in these observations is crucial in distinguishing a planet's mass from noise. Researchers addressed this issue by developing an execution of the REBOUND N-body code, which models the motion of objects within a gravitational field, to incorporate these fluctuations into calculations of planetary mass based on observables like a radial distribution function. Notably, this REBOUND implementation achieved a 10 times faster execution speed compared to existing methods, making it practically applicable to observations of multiple systems, as demonstrated through simulations of 10 to 200 planets. This improvement in speed enables researchers to rely more heavily on statistical approaches, as they found that various algorithms yield comparable results. Therefore, the implementation of these algorithms within REBOUND provides a reliable basis for these statistical analyses. The researchers' goals were motivated in part by ongoing GRISM observations of the multiple system KP-41G, which could potentially yield accurate detections of planets through microlensing techniques. To verify the reliability of their approach, they carried out extensive injections of synthetic planets and observed that most retained their actual mass within a 10% margin, except for extremely low-mass planets < 0.1 M Earth, which were occasionally misidentified with a 30% margin. The researchers further analyzed various factors influencing REBOUND's performance, such as up-scattering, perfect un-scattering, and elastic scattering, as well as the impact of observing angles and various N-body scenarios, which they found can be efficiently handled through machine learning. The researchers then compared REBOUND's performance with other codes, including Mercury and SYMPL, as part of a broader effort to standardize planetary mass calculations. Based on their analysis, they estimated a 30% deviation between these codes under various observing conditions, which they found can be significantly reduced by employing algorithms capable of efficiently simulating large numbers of particles. One such algorithm, the Guided Genetic Algorithm, was found to be particularly suitable for this purpose and yielded accurate results at a fraction of the computational cost. The researchers then applied their approach to analyze observed data from the GRISM plane of sight around KP-41G, using the Guided Genetic Algorithm to model and deduce the masses of multiple systems based on this data. In living organisms, the balance of ion concentrations across cell membranes is maintained by sophisticated molecular machines that transport ions in both directions. As these machines operate according to quantum mechanics but are studied in a context that is fundamentally classical, a quantum-based model is developed to analyze their regulatory mechanisms. This model, drawn from the study of quantum Brownian motion, forms the basis for a comprehensive mathematical equation that describes how the probability distribution of system states changes over time. By applying this equation to specific scenarios involving single ion channels, researchers find that quantum effects can in fact lead to notable changes in how cells respond to stimuli. This discovery opens up new possibilities for the study of how cells respond to signals in a wide range of biological contexts. For example, it is possible that quantum principles played a role in the original evolution of sensory systems that were essential for life on Earth. Even today, these principles may still influence how accurately cells can detect and respond to environmental signals.
