The ability of neural networks to learn exact wavefunction representations for quantum many-body systems is well-documented, yet in practice, severe limitations often apply. In the case of systems like the Hubbard model, severe constraints are imposed due to the sign problem that arises, making it difficult to develop useful approximations. Despite this limitation, recent breakthroughs have revealed that certain architectures can still learn highly accurate representations. In this work, we explore the potential of using complex-valued neural networks to bypass these constraints and learn exact wavefunctions for the Hubbard model without being hindered by the sign problem. Our results demonstrate that using such networks, it is possible to develop highly accurate representations, approaching the exact limit, without being affected by the sign problem. In contrast, similar efforts with real-valued networks have shown a rapid decline in accuracy as the system size increases. Furthermore, our findings also show that using more stringent constraints, such as the sum-of-squares norm, can actually improve learning outcomes and lead to more accurate representations. Our research paves the way for the development of more effective algorithms to tackle challenging many-body systems. In particular, we show that this increased capability can be translated to a significant reduction in the computational cost of finding exact energy ground states. In a related development, we also identify a relationship between the number of hidden layers in neural networks and the computational size of symmetrized Hubbard lattices. Our research findings are expected to have far-reaching implications for fundamental research in quantum physics. In particular, we show that our discoveries can be utilized to tackle intricate problems like the quantum simulation of homogeneous Bose-Einstein condensates and the determination of phase diagrams for various phases. This leads to a Higgs doublet mass and results in a hierarchy in flavon masses, with the heavier ones exceeding the electroweak scale. We've developed two composite flavon-higgs frameworks, one featuring a global $SU(4)$ symmetry and another with a global $U(3)\times U(3)$ symmetry. In the $SU(4)$ framework, flavons and the Higgs form a singlet Dirac fermion, allowing for a natural hierarchy in flavon masses. In the realm of software development, frameworks serve as blueprints, facilitating multiple systems to be built using identical structural components. This promotes consistency and enhances the maintainability of codes. Within theoretical computer science, frameworks find application in transversal logic, where they help in generalizing proof strategies across diverse problems. However, the concept of frameworks becomes complicated when dealing with unverifiable assertions, as demonstrated by a recent study on propositional proof systems. This research seeks to investigate whether there exists a universal framework for unverifiable assertions, as evidenced by the proofs of specific problems. A notable example of such a framework is Frege, which is known to be sufficient for any logically sound statement. However, whether Frege is also necessary for all logically sound statements remains a pivotal question in the field. This research aims to address this query by identifying whether there is a minimal, Frege-exceeding framework for unverifiable assertions. We synthesize elements of robust learning and certifiable adversarial resilience into a comprehensive framework for robust Bayesian estimation. From this platform, we derive parameters for the mean and covariance of a Gaussian posterior distribution that can be accurately estimated even when confronted with adversarial examples. Notably, we are able to control the maximum possible deviation of the posterior parameters from their true values, thereby ensuring that this deviation remains within predetermined limits. Building on this framework, we develop a method for generating certifiable adversarial examples that are both effective and efficient. Specifically, we show that a limited number of queries to a learner and a tester are sufficient to produce instances that induce specified margins between classes. Finally, we investigate the theoretical limits of our approach, examining the minimum resources required to establish robust Bayesian estimation in the context of linear regression. Specifically, we establish that a certain level of convergence can be achieved with probability greater than zero, and that this degree of convergence is optimal in the sense that it cannot be surpassed by any other method. Moreover, we are able to approximate this level of convergence through an iterative process, and demonstrate that the resources necessary for this approximation scale sublinearly with the size of the dataset. These findings are substantiated through experimental evaluation of our approach on MNIST and CIFAR-10. Furthermore, we extend our framework to accommodate non-Gaussian posterior distributions, and apply our methods to the estimation of Gaussian Mixture Distributions, achieving results that are comparable to those of existing robust estimators. Ultimately, we are able to establish that our approach offers a balance of robustness, efficiency, and complexity that is superior to that of existing robust estimators. The code for our approach is available at https://github.com/yotamgrinberg/CAR_Bayesian_Estimation. This research is based on arXiv preprint [1901.04377] and [2002.04268]. It has been published in IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems, and is currently being published in Neural Information Processing Systems.

In early 2020, as the COVID-19 pandemic spread across China, digital rumors began to circulate on Chinese social media platforms, posing a significant threat to public safety and stability. To combat this issue, Chinese authorities launched a special campaign to counter misinformation. Our research analyzed the spread of these digital rumors across different social media platforms in China, and how they were addressed by the authorities. We found that, unlike the situation with the 2003 SARS epidemic, misinformation spread quickly in China, largely due to the lack of accurate information from official sources. However, once the authorities took action, the spread of these rumors was halted. Our study also revealed that, in contrast to Western social media platforms, Chinese users primarily rely on official sources of information and are less likely to engage with rumors, even when they benefit from them, as their primary goal is to show support and loyalty to the government. Our findings suggest that, in countries with similar digital environments, disseminating misinformation on a large scale may not be feasible, and that, in order to understand the spread of rumors, it is necessary to study the specific context in which they are spread and consumed. Additionally, our results imply that, in counter-measures against misinformation, it may be more effective to focus on promoting the dissemination of accurate information, rather than solely targeting rumors head-on. Finally, our study highlights the need for further research into the nature and goals of digital rumors, as well as their impact on public opinion and behavior, particularly in countries with strict information control policies, such as China. Starting from a set of fermions with nearest-neighbor hoppings, we establish a formal relationship between the parquet theory's higher vertex functions and the coefficients of a related Hamiltonian's expansion in terms of the electron number operator. This relationship enables parquet theory's self-consistent equations to be reinterpreted as those obtained from a related class of Hamiltonians that generalize the Hubbard model. We discuss how this new perspective's framework incorporates electron interactions via exchange of bosonic coefficients, leading to the formation of any number of fermionic holes. As a specific example, we demonstrate how this viewpoint predicts the emergence of spinless fermions when two hole holes interact within a two-boson framework. This prediction aligns with recent findings from parquet theory that it accurately describes when spinless fermions arise. Furthermore, we discuss how our formalism's extension to higher-dimensional lattices may offer a pathway to investigate topological properties in these structures. However, we note that parietal symmetry may be lost in our analysis due to the absence of flux attachment. Consequently, we propose that the parquet theory's results could serve as useful guidelines for the identification of topological properties in extended systems. Ultimately, we conclude that the reinterpretation of parquet theory provides a fresh perspective that may complement and potentially supplement the existing understanding of many-body physics provided by the Luttinger liquid framework. Additionally, we speculate that the theory may have the potential to investigate a broad array of electronic states, extending beyond spinless fermions, as well as superconducting, superfluidic, and Mott insulating states. Lastly, we present various ideas on how the parquet theory's framework could be modified to describe these additional many-body states in a self-consistent manner. These concepts are anticipated to be developed into a full theoretical program in the future.

The pervasive nature of electronic media in recent centuries has further contributed to this phenomenon. The mainstream availability of audio recordings has enabled widespread exposure and synthesis of musical ideas from diverse sources.

This is followed by an in-depth examination of how Western popular music has evolved over the past 115 years. Our findings reveal two major shifts in its data complexity. We compare these results with the findings of a previous study and contextualize them within the broader cultural trends of the past millennium. The discussion concludes with an exploration of the possible causes of these changes. 

We demonstrate the efficacy of our data complexity metric by using it to characterize the distinct characteristics of different musical genres and artists. Additionally, plotting the data complexity of songs against their release years reveals intriguing patterns. Moreover, our analysis reveals that the most influential artists tend to release music with increasing complexity as their careers progress. 

To further validate our approach and identify specific trends, we applied a statistical time-series analysis to our data. This revealed two significant periods of change - one around the 1930s and another in the 1960s and 1970s. Our analysis also identifies potential correlations between musical complexity and societal factors, revealing a possible link between the complexity of music and cultural norms surrounding technology and politics. 

The discussion concludes by highlighting the potential applications of our approach and the significance of exploring the evolution of music as a complex system. Future studies can build upon our work by incorporating more comprehensive datasets, applying alternative metrics, and delving into the finer details of song-level complexity.

We've obtained a straightforward yet reliable approach to determine how many times a certain sequence of numbers is likely to occur within a set of random data. Our method is straightforward because it's essentially the same as comparing the sum of these random data to a predetermined threshold using a standard probability scale, and it's reliable because it's based on long-term averages of the data. One benefit of this approach is that it doesn't rely on specific assumptions about the data, beyond requiring that we're dealing with a certain type of random data, and it's easy to apply even when working with a large amount of data. We've applied our procedure to identify rare patterns within large datasets. Our findings align with previous findings obtained using more complex procedures, and they suggest that certain patterns are significantly less likely to occur than others. We've applied our procedure to gain insight into how our brains identify meaningful patterns within the sensory data that our senses detect. Our approach is similar to the techniques used in machine learning to identify common patterns in data and is based on the same statistical concept as the 'law of large numbers.'

To tackle the sparseness and time-consuming nature of human labeling in reinforcement learning, we've developed a novel approach called Visually Supported Cluster Ranking (VSCR). VSCR utilizes deep neural network policies to create grouped actions based on their associated probabilities, then has human evaluators rate these clusters instead of individual actions. By doing so, VSCR enhances efficiency by reducing the required number of labels by a factor of 8-10. Our empirical results demonstrate that VSCR is a viable and efficient means of obtaining human feedback. Moreover, VSCR's rankings serve as a soft constraint during policy training, yielding better performance than methods ignoring human feedback or using it for simple reward learning. VSCR's performance benefits from the integration with other training techniques, such as policy distillation and multi-objective learning. VSCR has been successfully applied in two real-world projects involving the evaluation of a shopping assistant and a medical decision-making system. VSCR's source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/pcyin/VSCR. For example, when evaluating a shopping assistant, we obtained 1) high-level feedback on action clusters from hospital staff, and 2) a significant performance boost (~5.5% in success rate) after integrating human feedback into our model. This research investigates the formation of baroclinic waves in a rotating, horizontally extended cylinder using both numerical and experimental methods. A novel setup is introduced, where an air-filled cylinder is subjected to temperature gradients that trigger the onset of baroclinic waves. We examine the influence of wave amplitude as a function of rotating rate, with particular focus on how it differs from traditional Rossby wave behavior. Both models show that increasing the rotating rate reduces wave amplitude. However, the ratio of wave amplitude to the critical growth rate varies significantly between the two setups. Furthermore, numerical and experimental findings are compared, highlighting that experimental wave amplitudes are about 30% larger than those from the numerical model. It is suggested that this discrepancy arises from inaccuracies in representing the boundary layer in the numerical model. Additionally, we explore the potential for different baroclinic wave behaviors to arise from variations in inner and outer cylinder temperatures. In both models, altering temperature ratios leads to distinct dynamics, with numerical model simulations indicating multiple steady states exist for particular temperature combinations. However, further study is needed to confirm if these effects are also present in the experimental model. This research seeks to provide a benchmark for comparing different baroclinic wave models and theories. By pinpointing the sources of disagreement between numerical and experimental results, this study aims to facilitate future research in this area. Ultimately, we hope to shed more light on how baroclinic waves initiate and develop in spinning systems. With further analysis, this research may contribute to our understanding of how spinning systems become unstable through the lens of baroclinic waves. As such, we present our findings with the aim of stimulating additional investigations. Differing from traditional adversarial learning settings, this attack targets the reinforcement learning paradigm, which doesn't rely on direct adversarial interactions. Focusing on a specific variant of this problem – namely, the setting in which an attacker only corrupts a subset of the available training data, and not the policy itself – we develop a corruption-resilient offline reinforcement learning approach. In machine learning, particularly in natural language processing, assessing out-of-distribution (OOD) performance is crucial to preventing harmful biases and errors.  However, current methods are often unreliable because they fail to account for the diversity of OOD categories, making it difficult to generalize to real-world scenarios. 

Our research involves collecting a wide range of diverse OOD categories from multiple sources, including labels provided by crowdworkers and category names from public datasets. 

We then use these categories to fine-tune existing approaches to identifying OOD texts and propose a new metric, called the classification accuracy difference (CAD), which outperforms existing benchmarks.

Our work's key contributions are:

1. A comprehensive dataset of 19 distinct OOD categories derived from crowdsourced labels.
2. A new direction for OOD detection, involving the reduction of false positives within specific categories.
3. An improvement over existing benchmark performances through refined evaluation criteria.
4. An open-source repository hosting our code and data, at https://github.com/htrdd/oodDetect.
5. Experimental evidence supporting our hypothesis that generalizing across categories is challenging, with results showing that performance varies significantly depending on the target category.
6. An analysis highlighting the benefits of our proposed approach compared to current methods.
7. Preliminary findings indicating potential future improvements by integrating data enrichment techniques. 
8. An identification of the limitations and potential future risks of our work, involving the expansion of OOD categories and potential reliance on annotated data. 
With these contributions, we aim to advance the field and facilitate future research in OOD detection. 
Our proposed approach is compatible with most modern deep neural network based methods and can be adapted for other domains, such as out-of-distribution data detection in images and semi-supervised learning.

Developing self-propelled molecular machines at the Brownian scale is a daunting task, despite the theoretical foundation provided by a decades-old model describing the dynamics of tunneling through molecular barriers. These molecular engines, powered by an unconventional form of friction, defy construction using conventional control mechanisms. To overcome this challenge, a new approach is proposed, rooted in the idea that these molecular engines exist in a state of transient instability. This theoretical framework is tested by analyzing the dynamic behavior of a basic tunneling model and a more sophisticated representation of molecular barriers. As a result, design criteria are established that can facilitate the development of molecular engines capable of dynamic movement. (Authorized oral presentation at 2021 Nanoscale Symposium)

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995, primarily composed of hydrogen and helium, posed significant questions about its formation and evolution. Research focused on the properties of GJ 229B, particularly its low mass, low luminosity, and unusual composition, yielded mixed results. To resolve these questions, we applied the APOLLO chemical retrieval model to the planet-disk of the GJ 229 system, simulating the growth of a object from dust and ice particles. Our analysis considered the impact of various factors, including the C/O ratio, ice accumulation efficiency, and planetary mass. In graph layout designs, upward planarity is a key concept that refers to the ability to arrange a given graph's nodes in an upward direction without violating the principle of planarity that ensures the graph's edges do not intersect. We develop several methods to assist in the layout design of upward planarity, specifically exploring parameterized versions of the problem in relation to tree-width and path-width graph structures. These techniques can be broken down into two categories: the application of parameterized complexity theory and the utilization of constraint programming with a focus on parameterized issues. Additionally, we introduce two new parameterized complexity theory problems related to upward planarity, specifically examining the layout design in linear time for outerplanarity with fixed tree-width and the existence of a planar embedding with a restricted number of crossings for graphs with bounded path-width. Furthermore, we investigate how to efficiently solve some upward planarity layout design issues within the context of constraint programming with a focus on parameterized problems, specifically exploring the application of parameterized variants of the linear programming branch and bound method. These techniques are particularly useful for the solution of single-parameter problems, such as finding a layout that approximately approximates planarity with the fewest crossings. These solutions lead to the development of two new algorithmic alchemy allications: the establishment of a parameterized complexity theory problem related to upward planarity that is solvable in linear time and the design of a constraint programming solver with a parameterized issue. These developments are substantiated through empirical evidence and experimental analysis. Finally, we extend the applicability of these new methods to other graph layout design problems, such as the application of parameterized complexity theory and the utilization of constraint programming with a focus on parameterized issues in the design of fractal planarity, negative weight planarity, and embedding-free outerplanarity. These extensions are also substantiated through empirical evidence and experimental analysis. The research presented here introduces new algorithmic solutions for graph layout design problems, providing an extensive literature review on these problems. The developed techniques are implemented in an open-source software framework and tested through extensive empirical analysis. The results of this research are publicly available for other researchers to utilize and expand upon. In multi-step visual navigation tasks, agents encounter situations that can be resolved by recalling previously observed information.  We introduce MemoNav, a navigation method that selects relevant memories to guide visual navigation.  MemoNav represents a navigation episode as a graph of objects and attributes, where useful memories are connected to key objects.  By predicting memory relevance over time, MemoNav prioritizes the selection of more relevant reminders.  Through evaluation on a diverse set of benchmark datasets, MemoNav's performance surpasses state-of-the-art navigation models while reducing memory access.  Specifically, MemoNav outperforms NavNet+CelebA and Deep Net Navigation on the DeepMind Challenge Benchmark by 5.7% and 9.6% respectively, while simultaneously reducing memory accesses by 43.  Additionally, MemoNav successfully demonstrates the utilization of reminders in more complex scenarios.  The introduced approach outperforms previous methods while showcasing its potential in tackling intricate navigation problems. This study demonstrates the importance of data validation in machine learning, particularly when working with data from unverified sources like publications in fields such as medicine and social science. To facilitate data validation, we created SEM-TAB-FACTS, a new fact validation and proof discovery task focused on analyzing tables from scientific papers. In SemEval-2021, participants participated in two subtasks related to SEM-TAB-FACTS. The first task involved identifying whether the data in a table accurately reflected a real-world phenomenon, while the second task entailed identifying supporting evidence for a specific claim contained in the table. In total, 25 teams entered the competition, submitting 49 distinct submissions in accordance with the official data format. In contrast to our initial expectations, a small team, named ProveIt Dev Team, submitted all the successful entries for the first task, while multiple teams submitted entries for the second task. In total, we received 49 submissions, which met the official data format requirements, and a notable aspect was that none of the teams submitted incorrect data. We evaluated the submissions for both subtasks using two metrics: F1 score for task 1 and mean average precision at k=5 for task 2, and based on these evaluations, we found that the top three submissions for task 1 had perfect scores, whereas the top three submissions for task 2 had nearly perfect mean average precision values. In particular, the top submission for task 2 had a mean average precision value of 0.9786. Our analysis of the results from task 1 showed that teams performed particularly well when working with tables containing numerical data, whereas those submitting entries for task 2 faced more difficulty when dealing with tables from fields such as medicine and social science. To address this challenge, we made the official data available to the public and received feedback from experts in the field, who suggested several improvements to the dataset, including adding more annotated tables, utilizing data from relevant external sources, such as clinical trials, and developing a more sophisticated system for identifying supporting evidence. In the future, we aim to build upon the progress made in SEM-TAB-FACTS, particularly in proving the accuracy of data, as proven by the top submissions for task 1. Similarly, in task 2, we plan to enhance our proof discovery method by incorporating more sophisticated techniques and utilizing a more comprehensive dataset. By achieving these goals, we believe that SEM-TAB-FACTS will make a significant contribution to the field of fact validation in table data.

Decision trees and related classifiers have broad applications due to their ease of implementation, high interpretability, and ability to capture non-linear relationships. However, they are not well-suited for handling situations with significant ambiguity, particularly when certain conditions must be met for classification to occur. In such cases, other models like probabilistic quantified constraint solvers may be more effective, but they can be computationally intensive and difficult to interpret. This study presents a new approach, calling it Indecision Forests, that combines the strengths of decision trees while addressing limited representational capabilities due to ambiguity. Our proposed method relies on the ACAR system to handle quantified ambiguity in multi-label classification tasks. In our experiments, Indecision Forests outperformed decision forests and probabilistic solvers, often by substantial margins, and exhibited improved computational efficiency compared to probabilistic solvers. A detailed explanation and accompanying code are available on GitHub. Our model demonstrates the capability to learn from training data a sophisticated decision strategy, found to be particularly effective in our evaluation. This research was influenced by discussions at the 2022 Bellairs workshop on Knowledge Engineering. Our model's source code can be accessed at https://github.com/jamiewu/indecision_forests. A video presenting our work is available at https://youtu.be/6R3D9R9R3uo. Our model shows promise in addressing the limitations of decision trees while acquiring complex reasoning strategies under ambiguity. Future directions for Indecision Forests include applications in natural language understanding and data streams, as well as exploration of other acquisition methods. In particular, we envision Indecision Forests as a versatile tool for a broad range of domains, given its ability to learn under specific types of ambiguity. Our model's performance in acar forests compares favorably to existing methods, highlighting its potential as a versatile addition to the domain of concept learning. In particular, we believe Indecision Forests could be effectively integrated into existing knowledge-based systems, as its simple decision tree structure facilitates easy interpretation and extension with other reasoning methods. While our study focused on multi-label classification, we envision Indecision Forests to be a valuable tool for a range of tasks, including ranking and clustering. Our model's acquisition mechanism also raises questions about the relationship between predictability and decision theory. PrunedDTW has emerged as a highly efficient algorithm for time series similarity search. Building on PrunedDTW, this research introduces an enhanced variant called Early Discarding PrunedDTW (EDPD). This variation refines PrunedDTW by eliminating two key limitations, thereby increasing its computation efficiency. Initially, EDPD optimizes PrunedDTW's search pattern to achieve parallel execution. Subsequently, EDPD enhances PrunedDTW's early discarding capability. Through theoretical analysis and experimental validation, this research demonstrates that EDPD surpasses PrunedDTW in performance. Furthermore, the researchers have successfully applied the proposed EDPD technique to the demanding task of time series similarity search. Notably, the results of extensive experiments reveal that EDPD consistently outperforms PrunedDTW and the widely used RawDTW by a significant margin, with a remarkable 10 times faster search time in complex scenarios. In light of these findings, the researchers have made their source code available to the public, in order to facilitate the adoption of EDPD in real-world applications. In software testing, instructors typically assess students' understanding of concepts by inquiring about their thought processes and receiving detailed feedback on their actions. While receiving feedback is essential, instructors can also utilize student responses to deliver more targeted feedback. This empirical research compares the effectiveness of these two methods by analyzing the performance of 135 students in a testing course who received either type of feedback from their instructor. Following the course, students' final project grades, knowledge assessments, and self-evaluations of their understanding were examined and showed that students who experienced less conventional feedback performed better in these areas. Additionally, students without conventional feedback demonstrated higher levels of conceptual competence and were more confident in their abilities. These results suggest that, in software testing education, instructors may prioritize inquiry-based, concept-based feedback over detailed feedback on student actions. Future research will investigate whether this preference is unique to software testing education. For more information, visit https://arxiv.org/doi/10.1145/3486330.3486340. 

Keywords: Software testing, education, conceptual feedback, conventional feedback, student performance, empirical study, survey and questionnaires. 

All data collected during this research, including final project marks, knowledge assessments, and self-evaluation results, are available at https://github.com/AmrYassin/TestEd-Data.

Understanding why a deep neural network made a classification decision is difficult. Recent studies suggest that explaining neural networks can make them more trustworthy. This research explores a new approach that combines concept analysis within a logic-based framework to provide clear explanations for deep neural network decisions. By defining crucial concepts within this framework, we translate neural networks into logic-based formulas, enabling the identification of essential variables responsible for classification results. This method is particularly effective for at-test scenarios in binary classification, although it comes at a higher computational cost compared to other state-of-the-art approaches. Notably, it has the capacity to handle complex, multi-layered neural networks, whereas other il-based methods are limited by this constraint. After reducing variables to their most concise representation, the results show that this method can provide more insight into neural network decisions compared to other explanation techniques. This research presents a new framework that integrates concept analysis and logic-based reasoning to provide clear explanations for deep neural networks. The full implementation is available at https://github.com/pesd/canode. Experimental results are available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9net.2022.1.01. Due to the computational costs associated with this method, it is best suited for explaining individual decisions rather than the entire network. Nonetheless, it demonstrates promise in providing more insightful explanations for deep neural networks. Specifically, it shows potential in domains involving conceptual analysis and logic-based reasoning. Potential future applications include (i) integrating this method with other explanation techniques to provide a more comprehensive understanding of neural network decisions and (ii) further developing this method to handle additional inputs, such as graphs and time series data. Based on the results, it is possible that this approach could offer more clarity on how, for instance, self-attention mechanisms contribute to decision-making in transformer networks. Ultimately, it is essential to continue exploring the limits of il-based explanation of neural networks and addressing the associated computational challenges to make deep neural networks more transparent. In this research, the influence of temperature on the epitaxial growth of Heusler layers onto graphene/sapphire substrates is examined. The study reveals that temperature modulates the equilibrium between distant, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy, with higher temperatures facilitating the transition from pinhole to van der Waells epitaxy. This transition is ascribed to the increased thermal energy causing Heusler layer defects during deposition, while the growth along with graphene layers indicates a significant role of van der Waals interaction in this process. The findings first document the occurrence of van der Waals epitaxy in the Heusler system and offer insights into regulating the epitaxial arrangement through temperature control.

To address this, our research focuses on profit-sharing arrangements between content and service providers to motivate network service quality enhancements. Furthermore, we identify parameters that influence both schemes and reveal that the profit-sharing ratios are sensitive to the initial network conditions. Our findings show that the content provider's profit is more affected by the profit-sharing ratio than the service provider's, while the service provider benefits more from the complex pricing model. Lastly, we determine the optimal profit-sharing ratios that maximize the overall profit of both content and service providers. Our proposed solutions can be applied to streaming and content delivery services to improve quality and reduce costs for both parties. Moreover, our study provides actionable insights for companies on how to distribute profits fairly and promote quality improvements through cooperative mechanisms. Its methodology can be adapted by companies to tailor their approaches according to their specific service policies and requirements. This integrated theory, known as 'quantum theory from first principles', defines the core concepts of quantum theory through basic axioms and develops a unique language to describe its components. A key challenge in this integrated theory is developing a suitable language to represent quantum states and operators. To address this issue, a specific type of mathematical structure, known as pre-Hilbert spaces, is being explored as a possible tool to describe the domain of quantum states. Specifically, this study defines a 2-categorical adjunction that establishes a connection between the category of pre-Hilbert spaces and the category of observables, providing a strong foundation for the integrated theory. This adjunction can be viewed as a lifting of the Stone-Gel'fand-Naimark duality through a process called '2-categorical lifting of adjunctions'. This lifting proves that any functor from the category of pre-Hilbert spaces to the category of commutative algebras, which corresponds to the Stone-Gel'fand-Naimark duality, is equivalent to a certain extension of the density matrix functor, a key result in quantum theory. This connection enables further examination of the embedding of quantum states and operators within pre-Hilbert spaces. More generally, this research contributes to the development of a mathematical framework for integrating categorical axiomatics. Its findings provide a strong foundation for the integrated theory to describe the core concepts of quantum theory. To demonstrate this, a simple example is given to show that the state space of a system consisting of two parts is a specific type of pre-Hilbert space. Its relationship with the tensor product of pre-Hilbert spaces was also identified. This research also developed a mathematical structure known as 'quantum configuration space', providing a broad framework for the integrated theory to describe the core concepts of quantum theory. Its application is demonstrated in two specific scenarios, the harmonic oscillator and the angular momentum system. Its relationship with the tensor product of quantum configuration spaces was also identified. This research also explored other tools and methods for integrating quantum theory, including the use of monoidal categories and 2-categorical adjunctions. This research focuses on investigating torus twists that are equitable under 2D crystallographic groups. A crystallographic group is defined as the direct product of a lattice group with a finite group. The goal is to find all unique twists on a torus that remain equitable under these types of groups. To approach this, we first divide the torus into equivalent regions based on the crystallographic group and label them. We then determine the possible twists that map these regions to themselves and establish the symmetry group of the resulting labeling. Similarly to the quasifiltering twists on a torus, we categorize the twists into two distinct types: Q-twists and non-Q-twists. We demonstrate that the Q-twists form a non-Faltings abelian polynomial torus group and determine the generators of its ideal. We also show that the torus twists which are equitable under its crystallographic group are in a one-to-one correspondence with the torus twists that commute with the action of that group. While neural networks can produce endless variations, their capacity for creative innovation is limited by the size and quality of the training dataset. To overcome this, we explore incorporating artist interviews as supplementary training data, extracting the essence of artistic intent and empathy through manual transcription. To demonstrate the potential of neural artistry, we generate four pieces using human-generated prompts based on artist interviews. However, we confront a challenge: neural artistry models - like GANs - are inherently adversarial and optimize pre-conceived metrics such as similarity to the training dataset, thus hindering their creativity. To resolve this, we present the concept of ArtSim, a novel metric enabling quantifiable comparisons between human and neural artistic abilities. To test our hypothesis, we develop a simple GAN-based neural artistry model and compare its output to actual artworks created by their respective human counterparts. Our analysis reveals that training neural artistry models to prioritize diversity in art generation leads to more innovative outputs, and that with sufficient data and adversarial training, neural artistry models can surpass human creations. In numerous fields, researchers utilize academic publications as a fundamental source of information.  The process of reading these publications is akin to an information-seeking dialogue between the reader and the author, with each side posing questions and receiving responses.  We undertook a study to map out this informational dialogue by analyzing a large dataset consisting of research papers and related questions, which were also answers provided in response to a query posed in a more general fashion.  Through an analysis of this dataset, we identified common patterns in the information-seeking dialogue and examined how these patterns compare with previous studies on question-answering.  Our analysis reveals that, in general, research papers encompass a broader spectrum of information compared to typical question-answering, with a greater emphasis on details within a specific context.  Additionally, we found that the context in which these papers are used influences the type of information that is most sought after.  We hypothesize that these differences arise due to variations in how human and automated agents engage with academic information.  Our full dataset has been made available for further exploration. 

Our analysis reveals that the structure of information within research papers leads question-answering to focus primarily on specific entities and their relationships, overlooking other crucial aspects of the domain itself.  To address this disparity, we propose two new strategies: 
1. Generalizing: Breaking down complex search queries into more broad-based inquiries, encompassing multiple related questions. 
2: Domain Digesting: Extracting summaries from the domain itself, providing a better understanding of its composition. 

Our study is comprised of three main components: 
1) initially constructing general questions from research papers, 
2) determining the relevance of answers to these questions, 
3) developing new question-answering strategies inspired by the information-seeking dialogue between researchers and readers, as seen in the composition of academic publications. 
In our analysis, we considered three research paper datasets (Semantic Scholar Corpus, ArXiv, and PubMed) and employed two automated information-seeking dialogue approaches (one based on information extraction and another on neural networks). 
Our results show that research papers as answers provide context essential for comprehending the domain, whereas question-answering often overlooks this context in favor of specific entity-based information. 
To bridge the gap, we provide two new methods: Generalizing and Domain Digesting, enabling the automatic transformation of question-answering into a more contextualized information-seeking dialogue. 
Our full code and dataset are available for further exploration.

Advances in computational psychiatry utilize machine learning (ML) to improve ADHD diagnosis, considering neuroimaging data an essential factor. Recent breakthroughs in ML capabilities, coupled with growing brain-related data, enable more accurate psychiatric diagnoses. Resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) is a key imaging technique utilized to investigate ADHD, as it helps relate brain functions to structure. However, rs-fMRI data complexity necessitates significant computational power to process. To overcome this challenge, this research proposes an innovative approach, starting with an essential step of reducing rs-fMRI data dimensionality. Subsequently, a model is designed to identify the most critical brain regions to optimize ADHD diagnosis, as opposed to blanket approaches involving entire rs-fMRI data. Initially, a study was conducted to compare the diagnostic capabilities of state-of-the-art ML models, including BERT and ResNet, when applied to rs-fMRI data versus combined rs-fMRI and text data. Following that, a model was created to identify critical brain regions, as the most successful models fail without sufficient expertise. Ultimately, the developed model's capabilities are evaluated, and promising future developments are explored, such as enhancing computational efficiency with weight pruning, and expanding beyond ADHD diagnosis to a broader range of mental disorders. In our research, we propose an epidemic SISI framework that models the spread of diseases by combining SIS and SI models, with distinct-time epidemic assumptions. Our findings reveal that under these assumptions, the epidemic equations can be reduced to a set of non-linear equations, which we solve analytically by transforming them into a combined SIS model. Our solution indicates that the final epidemic outcome depends on the value of a critical epidemic parameter, and we demonstrate that our distinct-time epidemic SISI framework is applicable to various epidemic timing scenarios. Our analysis shows that the epidemic curve follows a non-linear power-law pattern, and through numerical simulations, we validate our analytical findings. Additionally, our results are consistent with the observations of pandemic patterns in humans. With the ability to model distinct-time epidemic scenarios, our framework offers a valuable tool for understanding and interpreting the spread of diseases during both lockdowns and the subsequent relaxation of restrictions. Our study provides a solid foundation for further exploring the application of non-linear epidemic models in studying pandemic patterns. We investigate how electronic currents through non-equilibrium quantum Hall junctions respond to varying temperatures. In cases where electronic currents are influenced by interference effects, this interaction triggers thermoelectric responses. This can manifest as thermoelectric switching in the current direction triggered by temperature variations, along with controlled heat transfer between different parts of the system. Crucially, both the direction and strength of heat exchange can be independently manipulated. To understand our observations, we developed a simplified theoretical model, which explains how thermoelectric responses emerge from local voltage variations caused by local heat transfers. This places our findings in the broader context of quantum thermodynamics. In particular, we have demonstrated a form of thermodynamic cooling, where an heat engine is designed with components that only allow heat to escape in specific directions. This research paves the way for further exploration of the multiple roles that heat can play in the transport of electric current. It also opens up the possibility of self-regulating heat engines that can switch on and off in response to temperature fluctuations. Both of these features have the potential to significantly improve the efficiency of any future heat-to-work conversion technology. We have developed two different algorithms for approximating the von Neumann entropy of a mixed quantum state. Both algorithms work by first generating a approximate purification of the state, and then approximating the entropy based on the quantum conditional minimum multiplicity. The first algorithm is similar to one previously proposed by by Alon, Ben-Eltrur, and Szegedy, but our version has been adapted for use on quantum computers. The second algorithm is an entirely new solution that leverages the capabilities of quantum computers to efficiently solve a specific #P hard problem. Our results include evidence that both algorithms complete in a time proportional to $O(\log^2 N)$ on a quantum computer, with the first based on von Neumann's measurement theory and the second on a new principle of quantum cover. The second algorithm can also be used to approximate approximate entropy decay in a time proportional to $O(\log N + \Delta^2 N)$ on a quantum computer, with the ability to solve a specific problem on a classical computer in that time as well. This study addresses the challenge by developing a novel deep learning-based approach for semi-supervised ICD-11 category classification. The proposed method leverages the inherent structure within the taxonomy to generate new training data and employ contextual information, effectively reducing the reliance on extensive labeled datasets. The findings from our experiments, conducted using two large clinical datasets, demonstrate that our approach surpasses the performance of existing state-of-the-art techniques. A novel, two-phase approach for producing uniform spanning trees is presented, utilizing Wilson's method in the exploration phase and a straightforward technique in the exploitation phase. The latter technique leverages pre-generated trees to speed up the algorithm, and the overall strategy offers a balance of efficiency and speed. The paper demonstrates that the two-phase method can function without the Aldous-Broder algorithm, substituting it with another random walk-based method, the "choose-roots" algorithm. The resulting implementation is claimed to be the fastest to date for generating random spanning trees. The research also explores potential applications of the generated trees to model population growth and understand speciation. The findings are further illustrated with a range of simulated examples. The authors propose that the spanning tree method could be utilized to explore the "molecules-to-manufacturing" portfolio, an investment strategy centered on the pharmaceutical and biotechnology sectors. The research highlights that, in the long term, random trees tend to be more valuable than uniformly selected trees. The investigation shows that both algorithms produce similar results when used over a long period of time. The authors suggest that, in the long run, both methods demonstrate a proportional relationship with the harmonic series. The research also examines how the length of produced trees changes when using Wilson's method, revealing a power-law relationship. The authors claim that the resulting trees represent a universal model for understanding speciation, where tree genera are used as the primary specification. The research also explores the application of the spanning tree method to model population growth, where the challenge is to generate random trees with specified means. The investigation shows that both algorithms fail to produce trees with specified means when used over a long period of time. The authors propose that the exploration phase should be used to generate random trees with specified means, and then utilize the resulting trees in the exploitation phase to produce random spanning trees. The research highlights the potential benefits and drawbacks of the two-phase method, and claims that further investigation is needed to understand its potential applications and limitations. The authors claim that the two-phase approach offers a balance between efficiency and speed, and could be utilized as a general-purpose algorithm for generating random spanning trees. The behavior of dark solitons in Bose-Einstein condensates and optical systems with varying dispersion is analyzed through both theoretical and numerical methods. A specific model for optical systems, involving the combined effects of Kerr nonlinearity and variable dispersion, is shown to support stable dark solitons within a specific parameter range. Additionally, we examined the interaction between two solitons in this context and found that our system exhibits sufficient stability to support long-range soliton collision. Our research further revealed that small deviations in radiation pressure have a negligible impact on the overall stability of the solitons. This is evident from the small phase space area associated with these deviations. Furthermore, we explored the interaction between a dark soliton and a bright soliton in this new system and found the outcomes to be in good agreement with existing experimental findings. Our study also compared the stability of dark solitons in Bose-Einstein condensates with those in optical systems and found the latter to be more stable due to the presence of variable dispersion in the latter. This comparative analysis of stability is likely to be extended to other combinations of one-dimensional solitons in varying media. Our research provides insight into the stability of solitons in optical systems and offers potential applications for developing stable optical solitons based on dark solitons. This could be realized through the creation of stable dark soliton-induced optical waves. Moreover, our study of variable dispersion may find applications in the development of new optical wave propagation systems. This includes optical wave propagation over optical fibers with non-linear variable dispersion. Similarly, our research may also find applications in the development of variable dispersion based on photonic crystals and photonic wire systems. This includes the development and design of optical solitons in variable dispersion photonic crystal and photonic wire systems. Recent research using realistic simulations demonstrated that transport rates in a stellarator design are influenced by the natural fluctuations inherent in its non-axisymmetric configuration. To improve stellarator development, our study explores modifications to the coil placement pattern, identifying enhancements in plasma confinement through local optimization. These optimized designs exhibit improved energy gain, reduced exhaust divergence, and increased torque, indicating increased potential for stellarator configurations. Importantly, our findings reveal that the coherence of plasma fluctuations within these optimized regions increases, counter to expectations based on the natural stellarator chaos. Through detailed analyses of the plasma's spatial structure and the characteristics of its turbulence, we pinpoint the underlying features of these improved coil arrangements. Our research employs advanced simulation techniques to investigate the complex interactions between plasma and torque in novel stellarator designs, providing valuable insights for enhancing stellarator development. Additionally, these optimizations serve as a starting point for reducing the technical complexities and costs associated with transforming these designs into practical configurations for a fusion power plant. Given the general applicability of our design methods, our findings are likely to influence not only stellarator research but also the entire field of magnetic fusion. Furthermore, our study paves the way for further research into the extensive range of stellarator designs, promoting exploration of the numerous possibilities within this design space. Effective heat transfer between a solid and gas phase relies on rapid physical processes that govern convective and radiative heat transfer. 
A detailed understanding of these processes was obtained through MRI imaging of Bauxite sand heated by an air flow. 
Temperature and velocity measurements confirmed that heat transfer is optimized at high vibration amplitudes, and that convection dominates heat transfer at lower vibration levels. 
However, when vibration is introduced, heat transfer is largely facilitated through conduction within the bed itself. 
This understanding will contribute to developing more efficient heat transfer techniques.

I. Introduction
---------------

Rapid heat transfer between two objects is essential in many processes including food cooking, aircraft engines and energy production. 
When one object is stationary and the other is moving past it, the transfer of heat between the two can be both conductive and convective. 
Although the principles behind this process are complex, our experiments have shown that both the vibration of the solid object and the temperature difference between the solid and gas phases play important roles in the heat transfer between the two. 
Due to the rapid rates involved, studying these processes has been a significant challenge, but our use of MRI imaging has enabled us to observe and analyze the heat transfer between the stationary solid and moving gas phases in a number of configurations. 
In this study, we examined how the vibration of Bauxite sand, heated by an air flow, affects heat transfer and used MRI to visualize the temperature distribution within the bed itself. 
Based on our findings, we have explored the underlying physical processes involved and how they relate to the heat transfer between the two phases. 
Ultimately, our goal is to identify the most effective way to increase heat transfer between the two phases.

Biomolecular aggregates, such as amyloid fibrils, exhibit a universal tendency to
form independently of the specific protein sequence. Although differing in
their native structures, these proteins share a common thread of forming
hydrophobic regions when translated into their amino acid sequences. By leveraging
this similarity, our study explores the possibility of self-organizing systems
comprising multiple proteins that adopt a unique, collective configuration.
Through analytical calculations based on a minimal model, we show that when two
components with contrasting hydrophobic properties interact, they give rise to a
stable, ordered state. Notably, this order arises not from a predetermined
template but rather through the emergence of a shared template from the
interplay of the interacting proteins. Furthermore, our results indicate that
this ordered state is characterized by localized structures, akin to hydrophobic
cores, surrounded by disordered regions. Moreover, our model predicts that
these localized cores could be imbued with amyloid-like properties. Our work
reveals that the self-organization of biomolecular aggregates is a multifaceted
phenomenon and provides a potential framework for understanding the
self-assembly of proteins through a collective, emergent approach. Additionally,
this framework could act as a starting point for crafting artificial molecular
self-organization systems. Lastly, our study offers a generalizeable model that
could be applied across various domains to design modular, multi-component
systems exhibiting stable states with inherent structural characteristics.

The theory is based on a principle known as the b-principle, which splits flexible geometric problems into two simpler forms. We apply this theory to prove a key hypothesis proposed by David Mumford, thereby confirming his initial claims. The theory holds significant value in understanding geometric structures, and we utilize it to resolve this deeply mathematical hypothesis. Additionally, we explore an extension of the theory, referred to as the weak b-principle, which holds global implications. We provide a simple explanation for this extension using a fundamental concept called Poincaré polynomial. The proof of Mumford's hypothesis involves a combination of several key factors, including Poincaré polynomial, the b-principle, and a type of geometric structure known as self-duality. We provide a detailed explanation of these components as well as an extension of the theory, referred to as the smooth b-principle. We also utilize an elegant geometric concept known as the compactification to prove a related problem, specifically the case for singular points. We confirm that the combination of the b-principle and compactification has a profound effect on understanding geometric structures, as demonstrated by the confirmation of the hypothesis and other related results. Those who wish to understand the confirmation of the hypothesis may focus solely on sections 1-4, as the subsequent material involves more technical discussions. This work examines the robustness and efficiency of three multilevel preconditioning methods for cardiac mechanics simulations on hundreds of cores. It compares their performance on different models of heart failure, using commercially available software and tools. This study aims to identify the most effective approach for tackling complex cardiac mechanics problems with high-performance computing capabilities. From a computational mathematics perspective, we evaluate the feasibility of combining RIXM with Finite Element and Interface Fractional Stew methods. This research also explores the suitability of Flexible Parallel Multilevel Conjugate Gradient for such applications. It considers various factors like types of preconditioners, interfaces, and boundary conditions to replicate realistic scenarios. From a applications perspective, we investigate the impact of subdomain partitions, contact treatments, and kernel choices on the convergence of FEM computations. This trial utilizes 2048 cores to compare the convergence rates of eight distinct cardiac mechanics scenarios. Its findings suggest that MLPCG combined with RIXM upon MEA is the most efficient approach for such simulations. Furthermore, we have identified key factors influencing its performance, providing valuable insights for researchers and engineers to tune and enhance this technique for cardiac mechanics. Ultimately, we have established that MLPCG with RIXM represents a reliable and efficient solution for tackling a wide array of large-scale cardiac mechanics applications. This research contributes to the ongoing development of theardFEPCG software project, enabling the efficient FE solving of cardiac mechanics problems via parallel ML preconditioning of Jacobian matrices. This approach has been successfully tested, leading to considerable time savings in cardiac mechanics simulations. We look forward to further collaboration with the FE and PCG communities, continuing to refine and distribute theardFEPCG software via GitHub. This publication is also available on arXiv, with corresponding documentation and code provided. This research examines user-generated tags across different social media platforms and categorizes them according to their purpose. We found that tags are predominantly used for information retrieval, accounting for 79.6% of all tags, with 12.6% used for documentation and the remaining 7.8% having no defined function. Considering the evolution of tagging practices over time, we noticed that early users of Wikipedia tagged categories more frequently than categories themselves, but this trend reversed as the system grew. Through the analysis of tag propagation, we revealed a central role for major information hubs in distributing tags across related pages. Notably, 58% of tags on a given page originate from its top 1% most active contributors. Our findings provide insight for designers seeking to optimize social tagging systems and encourage effective participation. By identifying key factors and dynamics, we can design interventions to enhance tagging practices, such as encouraging collaboration through color-coded tags or time-based tagging guidelines. Overall, social tagging systems rely on the efforts of a relatively small group of information specialists. By recognizing and embracing this dynamic, we can refine these systems to produce more accurate metadata and support efficient information retrieval.

This paper examines the long-term behavior of solutions to the two-dimensional compressible FENE dumbbell model. We first establish the global existence of solutions for large initial data, then demonstrate that the solutions obtained are durable and affect the overall dynamics of the system. Finally, we prove that the solutions achieve a state of equilibrium over considerable time. In the process, we find that the alignment of the dumbbells converges to a specific distribution, which we call the equilibrium configuration. Additionally, the pressure in the fluid has converged to its correct value. Our analysis includes a key commutator estimate that allows us to prove the convergence of the alignment of the dumbbells over extended periods. This study offers evidence that non-linear stability holds for the equilibrium state of the 2-D compressible FENE dumbbell model. In the context of the model, we find that the convergence of the alignment of the dumbbells is the primary factor that drives the long-term behavior of the solutions. Furthermore, our work includes a detailed investigation of the physical properties of the solutions, which includes the non-negativity of the density and the correct dimensionless drag coefficient of the dumbbells. When multiple machine learning algorithms are compared, the process often involves optimizing and fine-tuning their hyperparameters through a process called global optimization. This study leverages the analysis of global sensitivity to evaluate and compare the optimal hyperparameters of genetic and particle swarm optimization algorithms in conjunction with three leading rankings: the Pareto front, the lattice-based ranking, the sorted criterion-based ranking, and the tie-breaking ranking. By utilizing Sobol's method to analyze the sensitivity of these rankings to variations in hyperparameters, researchers identified the most influential settings. This investigation analyzes the sensitivity of all rankings simultaneously to understand which hyperparameters have the greatest impact across all methods. Additionally, researchers focused on the sensitivity of each algorithm's top ranking to understand which hyperparameters affect each method uniquely. Reinforcement Learning (RL) is gaining significant traction as a research area, 
which means there's a rising need for comprehensive evaluation platforms to 
assess RL algorithms across various scenarios. Unlike static benchmark suites, 
a robust evaluation ecosystem should be adaptable to evolving research questions, 
provide precise control over simulation settings, and offer repetitive, repeatable 
evaluations ensuring reproducibility. This paper introduces L2Explorer: a RL 
evaluation platform that meets these demands by hosting a diverse collection of 
over 70,000 simulation runs based on 56 research protocols across multiple domains, 
enabling researchers to explore existing knowledge and gain insights into the 
progress of RL research. Furthermore, L2Explorer's infrastructure is designed to 
be scalable to support an increasingly vast corpus of knowledge as RL research 
continues to advance. This paper outlines the platform's conceptual framework and 
presents an analysis of its evaluation results. Moreover, it highlights the benefits 
of empirical RL research and provides an overview of the progress seen in many 
areas of RL research over time. This information serves as a starting point for 
future RL research to be conducted within the L2Explorer evaluation platform. This 
evaluation platform is currently available to the public at 
https://www.learngym.org/explorer and https://github.com/learnym/learngym/tree/main 
extras/explorer. Additionally, the full version of this paper can be found at 
https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.09044. This research was funded by DeitTron AI Research 
as part of a DeiDAC initiative. DeiDAC aims to apply and study foundation ML 
through the lens of social science. This financial support is hereby acknowledged. 
Moreover, we would like to express our gratitude for the support received from 
DeiDAC to conduct this research. More information about DeiDAC can be found at 
https://www.deidac.org/. This research has been impact assessed as follows: 
In this research, we have conducted evaluations across multiple domains using 
general RL methods. Our findings show that current RL approaches perform well 
generalized to various scenarios as evidenced by our comprehensive evaluation 
results. This research did not employ specialized domain knowledge, instead 
utilizing widely available publicly accessible data and domain-specific 
publications. Furthermore, our research has contributed to the accumulation of 
evaluated experiences in various domains which could be useful to future RL 
researchers should they choose to conduct evaluations

This study demonstrates the existence of traveling waves near Couette flow for the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations in the whole plane, provided the velocity field is smooth and its horizontal velocity component has a finite derivative. These waves correspond to asymptotically stable solutions of oscillating travelng waves. Additionally, we prove that as the viscosity coefficient becomes extremely small, these waves maintain a finite distance from a particular class of solitary waves over sufficiently long periods. Our analysis is based on a combination of techniques drawn from the study of quasilinear PDEs, as well as recent works on the behavior of solutions near equilibrium states and the properties of Gevrey functions. These results were conceptualized during conversations held at the Institut Henri Poincaré in Paris during a 2017-2018 semester dedicated to fluid dynamics. They were further discussed at the MSRI program on mathematical aspects of fluid dynamics at Stanford University.

This study's primary objective is to provide evidence and disproofs for the deterministic Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation including non-local slope-related terms, such as the generalized KPZ equation with "downward" and "upward" differences. We use a combination of mathematical approaches, including existing works on 1D nonlinear equations, to explore the local and nonlocal properties of these equations. We demonstrate that the local version of the equation possesses a unique solution in any given function space, while the nonlocal version does not have a solution for all function spaces. We also prove that the local version is robust against small perturbations in its initial condition and data, which is in line with the findings of previous studies. Conversely, we provide a counterexample that shows the nonlocal version is not robust against small perturbations in its initial condition and data. We also provide further evidence and disproofs for the nonlocal "upward" difference equation. Specifically, we prove that the nonlocal "upward" difference equation with a particular type of nonlinearity possesses a unique solution in any given function space, which is similar to the findings of previous studies. We also use these results to provide further evidence and disproofs for other related equations, such as the "upward" difference equation. We employ two main types of mathematical approaches, namely the "conical box" approach and the "branching property" approach, to prove these results, which are similar to the findings of previous studies. We also use these results to provide further evidence and disproofs for other related equations, such as the "upward" difference equation with a particular type of nonlinearity. More detailed descriptions of these approaches and other related works are provided in the reference section of this study. We also make some comparative observations on how these results are related to the findings of previous studies in the field of stochastic KPZ equation. The COVID-19 pandemic, categorized as a global health crisis by WHO, revealed a severe gap between the need for timely, accurate data and the ability to procure it. In the midst of an unfolding emergency, gathering and analyzing complete data becomes impractical, causing public health officials to rely heavily on anecdotal evidence. A combination of accessible public APIs and temporal analysis was employed in this research to fill the data void in South Africa. By using time-stamp aware methods on existing data sources, including Twitter and Google Trends, this study generated COVID-19 related temporal profiles. Subsequent proximal and distal analysis of these datasets indicated a 44-day lag between South African and global peak values, consistent with previously reported figures. Results also showed that Twitter data often predicted Google Trends data by 12-24 days. Consequently, non-intrusive methods of data collection can serve as viable public health tools, supplying essential insights to guide critical pandemic decision-making. Moreover, integration of machine learning algorithms could potentially enhance the predictive efficiency of these platforms. Ultimately, this research capstone caps off a series of studies examining the utility of social media in predicting disease trends since 2015. Given its straightforward approach, this study may provide a useful template for fellow Capstone teams seeking to apply similar methodologies in the future. Documents containing the code and data required for this replication can be accessed via github.com/AmukheResearchGroup2020/COVID-19-Repo under a strict adherence to licensed terms. Moreover, since COVID-19 was unforeseen, this research was conducted in harmony with the newly introduced guidelines from March 2020, solely relying on publicly accessible data and urging the use of existing data sources to guide the epidemic. This research does not possess any real-world implications that could potentially harm individuals, as it solely involves the analysis of publicly available data. Nevertheless, in the interest of transparency, I have substituted certain sensitive data with artificial values, while retaining its count. Let $A$ be a non-empty set of integers, and let $S_1 \subseteq A, S_2 \subseteq A, \ldots, S_{\lfloor \frac{4}{k} \rfloor+1} \subseteq A$. It is proposed that if the sums of the first $\lfloor \frac{4}{k} \rfloor+1$ smallest elements in the sets $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_{\lfloor \frac{4}{k} \rfloor+1}$ are the same, then there exist indices $i_1, i_2, \ldots, i_{k+1}$ such that the intersection of the sets $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_{k+1}$ contains an element $x$, and the equality $x + i_1 + \ldots + i_{k+1} = 0$ holds. It is demonstrated that this hypothesis yields an $O(k^3)$-time algorithm for solving the Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture. Furthermore, a random example is given which shows that the time complexity of the resulting algorithm is indeed at least $\Omega(k^2)$, hence the addition of 1 to the existing bound is optimal. Additionally, by generalizing this concept, a new Freiman's 5k-9 conjecture is formulated. It is proven that the generalized Freiman's 5k-9 conjecture implies another, independent problem in the field of additive combinatorics, specifically the k-5 problem. As a result, it is shown that the Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture can be reduced to a more complex problem, the k-5 problem, which is also random and unproven, thereby linking two distinct ideas in additive combinatorics together. It is hypothesized that if a set $A$ contains less than $k+1$ elements, the sums of its elements will all be the same, implying that the k-5 problem can be solved by selecting the appropriate sets $S_1, S_2, \ldots, S_{k+1} \subseteq A$ with distinct elements. Consequently, it is shown that the Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture can be solved by solving the k-5 problem, demonstrating a key application where Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture can elucidate an independent problem

In medical contexts, combining information from diverse sources is often necessary 
for accurate diagnosis. This study explores various methods for merging different 
medical information types, specifically image-patient data and textual data. Our 
research focuses on developing innovative techniques to integrate these modalities 
and their applications to diagnostically challenging conditions, such as glaucoma 
and diabetic retinopathy. This work introduces novel approaches to the tasks of 
classifying glaucoma and combining image-text data for diabetic retinopathy 
classification, surpassing existing benchmarks in both cases. The proposed methods 
are then used to analyze the impact of varying data modalities on diagnosis and 
evaluate their effectiveness under different data availability scenarios. Lastly, 
comparative assessments are made of the performance of the implemented models 
against specialized medical expertise. All experimental findings are reproducibly 
accessible on an online GitHub repository. The proposed techniques exhibit excellent 
diagnostic accuracy and showcase their potential to be adaptable to a range of 
different diagnostic tasks and data sources. They also highlight the importance of 
considering data modality variability when making clinical predictions and the 
significance of medical image information in retinal pathology assessment. Vector 
quantized generative adversarial networks are utilized to integrate image information, 
while for textual data, the study employs a textual approach that embeds clinical 
notes into a shared vector space for combined analysis with optical coherence 
topography data. Our research demonstrates that, through innovative combined-analysis 
techniques, even previously isolated medical information types can yield 
exceptionally accurate diagnostic results. All code is publicly accessible on a 
GitHub repository: https://github.com/gsagl/eyeClinic. R. ritzel@imclinic.de,

X-ray images contain valuable information about underlying lung conditions, such as infections, that can be instrumental in predicting severe complications in patients. This knowledge can be utilized to identify high-risk patients and optimize care delivery during the COVID-19 pandemic. In an effort to support clinicians, developing AI-powered tools that leverage X-ray image data to forecast ICU admission status for COVID-19 patients is crucial. 

Research in this field typically employs shallow convolutional neural networks to analyze image data, but due to their limited capacity in learning complex patterns, their performance is subpar. In contrast, deep convolutional neural networks exhibit superior predictive capabilities in various medical and image classification tasks. 

Building on existing research, this study proposes a characteristic-based approach to forecast ICU admission based on X-ray image data, utilizing a composition of deep convolutional neural network and decision tree algorithms. 

Specifically, multi-head attention was applied to broaden the deep convolutional neural network's capacity, effectively increasing the number of trainable parameters. When combined with a decision tree, this proposed approach demonstrates exceptional accuracy in predicting ICU admission, surpassing state-of-the-art shallow convolutional neural network models. 

Evaluation results indicate that our characteristic-based model is 2-4% more accurate than shallow convolutional neural network models, while requiring significantly fewer trainable parameters. Moreover, our approach generates a probabilistic outcome, enabling healthcare systems to weigh the uncertainty and make informed decisions during the COVID-19 pandemic. 

Code and pre-trained models for this study are available at https://github.com/jjy Yang/COVID-Unet. Additionally, our results have been uploaded to the COVID-19 Classification Benchmarks platform at http://covid-19-classification-benchmarks.kazemha.org/model/162546895/.
