The success of Deep Learning (DL) technology heavily relies on the development of efficient neural networks. In the context of point cloud analysis, researchers have explored various approaches to graph convolution, which is a crucial component of DL. Due to the irregular structure of 3D point clouds, designing an effective graph convolutional neural network presents significant challenges. This paper provides a comprehensive review of these methods, including their advantages and limitations, and introduces a simple benchmark suite to evaluate their performance. Furthermore, we introduce a novel, scalable protocol for training graph convolutional networks on large datasets, which serves as a standard for comparative evaluations. This protocol comprises three key components: an automatic generation method for approximate nearest neighbor graphs, a data augmentation technique, and a protocol for evaluating generalization performance. Our experimental findings reveal that many state-of-the-art graph convolutional networks excel on specific tasks but struggle with generalization, whereas simple and fundamental designs demonstrate more robust performance across multiple evaluation metrics. This research aims to identify key design principles and provide insights into the potential causes of these results. Additionally, we make our benchmark suite, source code, and generated approximation graphs available to the public to foster further research and development. This allows the research community to repeat our experiments, modify our approach, or simply explore our findings as a starting point. Our aim is to promote collaboration and accelerate breakthroughs in point cloud analysis through DL. Moreover, we seek to educate RAGS* about best practices in graph convolutional neural networks by highlighting their weaknesses and providing simple, effective designs as examples. *RAGS stands for Research As Much As Greedy Scientists.

Trojan assault, a subtle form of cyber deception, hides within program inputs, waiting to trigger when a certain condition is met, resulting in significant damage. To carry out this type of attack, malicious code is embedded in a program, concealed from its control flow system. Recent advances in deep learning have enabled researchers to devise new, more sophisticated forms of Trojan assault. Specifically, hostless Trojan assault techniques, such as Text-Based Trojan assault, have been explored, where the trigger condition originates from the input data, and the trigger can be specified through natural language. Nevertheless, existing approaches still rely on program source code and require linguistic inputs to be translated into actual data, and the translation process is done manually, and the semantic meaning of the input data is not fully considered. In this research paper, we introduce Semantic Hostless Trojan Assault, the first of its kind, where the Trojan assault trigger is specified using semantic descriptions of data, and we propose two such forms of this type of attack, namely Textfelt and Cartelan. Furthermore, we present practical implementations of these attacks on two common datasets, and we evaluate their effectiveness, revealing that they surpass existing Text-Based Trojan assault techniques. Moreover, we investigate the robustness of these attacks against common defense strategies. Our research findings indicate that these new forms of Trojan assault are more formidable, and our code is publicly available on this GitHub repository https://github.com/tajani2/SHTA. Our research aims to convey that deep learning-based semantic representations can be leveraged to carry out highly effective Trojan assault attacks. Additionally, we found that existing Text-Based Trojan assault attacks can be surpassed significantly. Moreover, we discovered that common defense strategies are ineffective against these new forms of Trojan assault. Lastly, we found that these new forms of Trojan assault can be carried out without any need for knowledge of the program source code. Our research findings are expected to contribute significantly to the fields of deep learning, semantic processing, and cyber security. These low core ratios are consistent with the migration hypothesis, where many planetary systems may have encountered and interacted with other planets during the late stages of planetary formation.  A comparison with our solar system reveals notable differences, where Mercury and Mars have core-to-mass ratios of 0.55 and 0.14, respectively.  The absence of large core-sized planets in our analyzed sample, particularly in the low-metallicity group around GKM stars, implies that many such planets may have encountered and interacted with other objects in their final orbital destinations, leading to the reduction in core size through erosion processes.  Additionally, it is suggested that the diversity in internal compositions of exoplanets may be closely tied to the diversity in chemical compositions among their host stars, where planets formed in super-solar metallicity environments tend to have smaller cores than those formed in less metal-rich environments. As a result, the positioning performance does not fully utilize the available CSI. To address this issue, we propose using the attention mechanism within the DNN architecture to weight CSI according to its confidence level. This is done by calculating the attention weights for each CSI by taking the inner product between the feature map of the current layer and the extracted features from an attention module. The proposed system consists of a common part that extracts common features from the CSI and multiple path aggregations that calculate the position by fusing the weighted CSI. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed system outperforms the traditional DNN and multi-layer perceptron (MLP) methods. Additionally, we found that the geodesic distance is a better distance metric for positioning than the Euclidean distance and that the proposed system achieves better convergence than the DNN and MLP methods. Building on the framework of category theory, we define a modal logic for arbitrary spaces, offering a more abstract and general framework than traditional modal logic. In this context, we examine the integration of modal logic operators and demonstrate the equivalence of this categorical approach with traditional modal logic methods. In particular, we define topological analogues for the Forth and Back operators and establish their universal properties within the framework of subobjects. Our results are applied to both sober and weakly-sober topological spaces. Additionally, we will explore how these ideas relate to hydra structures, an abstract representation of composability that can be applied to both subobjects and ideals within a given ring. This study explores how centralised models in multi-agent systems cope with distributed data and potential network disruptions. We introduce a reliable learning approach that incorporates regional queries to mitigate the effects of disconnected agents. A theoretical framework outlines the conditions under which local and global information exchange through centralised models facilitates consistent decision-making despite network disruptions. Empirical analysis on synthetic data confirms that centralised models with regional training have superior performance and faster convergence compared to other distributed learning methods. Furthermore, our reliable approach has comparable computational overhead to standard distributed learning techniques. We demonstrate the viability of our approach in large-scale systems comprising up to 20,000 agents. Our research shows that centralised models with regional training and diverse data can achieve high generalisation beyond the learned regions. This knowledge can be utilized to devise more effective strategies for resilient distributed learning. The associated code can be accessed via https://github.com/jbme-epfl/rellearn.

with attributes unlike any known brown dwarf, showing infrared colors 
distinctly red, possibly indicating the presence of a massive dust cloud. 
Initial data suggested this object is young, with an age of around 10 million years.

distance, and lack of significant optical and near-infrared emission.

We propose an effective scheme for the interpolation and progression of parton distribution functions. This approach utilizes both global and local PDF fits alongside ensemble averaging to achieve more accurate results. By applying this method to the case of the nucleon PDF, we discover that using PDF ensembles from different renormalization schemes can significantly enhance the accuracy of the interpolation. Nonetheless, the improvement is minimal when using different evolution parameters. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of quark flavor mixing on the progression of PDF and found that it leads to enhanced discrepancies between various PDF sets, particularly at high parton momentum fractions. Additionally, we studied how different fitting boundaries in DGLAP evolution affects the progression and found that using a fitting boundary beyond $x \sim 5$ leads to enhanced discrepancies when compared to using a boundary at $x \sim 5$. Lastly, we explored the behavior of the valence-like distribution function $xG(x)$ for different PDF ensembles and observed that using an ensemble average or progression from DGLAP boundaries other than the NNPDF3.1 ensemble leads to increasingly negative $xG(x)$ at low $x$ values, which we attribute to issues arising from the fitting process and progression of PDF. In contrast, the PDF ensemble approach produces $xG(x)$ results that are in closer agreement with existing experimental data. Our work paves the way for further research into the issues surrounding PDF progression and the applicability of the ensemble approach. It also underscores the importance of including valence-like distribution functions in global PDF fits to mitigate potential issues. Moreover, we observed that using an effective PDF progression can result in more accurate PDF estimates for complex renormalization schemes such as NRQCD. Finally, we identified key areas for further exploration in the field of PDF progression. This research is expected to be continued in a forthcoming publication. In the interim, we are making available to the public all the PDF sets used in this study, which can be accessed via the website pdf4LHC.org. These PDF sets are also scheduled to be uploaded to the LHPC repository. Our work is anticipated to contribute meaningfully to the ongoing discussion of PDF progression within the PDF for LHC4 community. It is based on earlier research conducted by the PDF4LHC collaboration, which is led by J. Gao, with key contributions also from S. Carrazza, R. Bougton, and Z. Zhang. Our study draws heavily from the work of J. Chaves, M. Herrero, and A. Nakamura.

By analyzing a small sample of 15 galaxies at a redshift of 0.04, we are comparing star formation rates derived from spectroscopic data on the line Brackett-$\gamma$ against those obtained using SED fitting. Despite some uncertainty associated with the calibration of the narrowband observation, our results show a strong correlation between the two methods of estimating star formation rates. Furthermore, we are testing whether these two approaches are equivalent by considering the effects of dust and gas in the narrowband spectrum. Using data on narrowband colors and hydrogen recombination lines, we have developed a new method of calculating the contribution of dust and gas. Based on the analysis of our sample galaxies, the contribution of dust and gas appears to be negligible, confirming that the star formation rates derived from spectroscopic and photometric data are indeed equivalent. This leads us to anticipate that for a broader set of galaxies at higher redshifts, the contribution of dust and gas may also be negligible, thereby facilitating the use of narrowband observations as a quick and inexpensive way of determining their star formation rates. However, we also acknowledge the possibility that for galaxies at redshifts beyond 1, the contribution of dust and gas may become significant, thereby complicating the interpretation of narrowband data. To confirm this hypothesis, further research will be needed using a larger sample of galaxies at a wider range of redshifts. The relationship between the contribution of dust and gas and redshift could potentially be influenced by another factor, with higher redshifts corresponding to greater contributions. Overall, our study is focused on understanding the complex effects of dust and gas in narrowband spectra, as well as the implications of our findings for future research into the calibration of star formation rates derived from spectroscopic and photometric data. Based on our analysis, we are estimating the contribution of dust and gas in a galaxy with extremely narrowband colors. This leads us to predict that at a redshift of around 1.5, the contribution of dust and gas may become so significant that it could actually cancel out the emission of narrowband radiation, thereby making it unobservable. Consequently, we do not expect our test of the relationship between narrowband colors and star formation rates to yield reliable results at redshifts beyond 1.5. Nevertheless, we are estimating the contribution of dust and gas for a galaxy with certain narrowband colors, as well as a certain star formation rate. Our findings are consistent with a previous prediction, with galaxies that form stars at a higher rate also having narrower narrowband spectra.

The equation for universal diffusion, first proposed by Anderson, Falk, and Soule, can be utilized to model traffic flow by combining it with the Greenberg equation, which assumes that drivers adjust their speed based on perceived headways. However, the resulting combined equation exhibits non-physical self-exploding solutions that contradict real-world expectations. To resolve this issue, we reformulate the combined equation through a different approach, which involves replacing the speed adjustment term with a more complex expression that takes into account the interplay between drivers' reactions and their visual perception of the road. This revised equation can be solved numerically and has been found to have unique, self-stabilizing solutions for any initial conditions, which align more closely with real-world traffic patterns. Moreover, we have observed similar properties in a similar combination of equations proposed by Whitham. Furthermore, we have explored various combinations of equations through numerical studies and have discovered that our proposed method yields universally applicable diffusion equations in nearly all cases. Therefore, we advocate for numerical methods as an effective tool for combining traffic models and universal diffusion equations. Our proposed method also displays analogous behavior in other physical systems, such as pedestrian flow modeling, and we present relevant numerical examples in this context. Finally, we acknowledge that our study raises significant theoretical concerns and suggests the need for further research to develop globally convergent methods for universal diffusion equations. Our work is comprised of two main articles, where the first article focuses on the numerical methodology and related issues, while the second article delves into the related theoretical and philosophical implications. Due to space constraints, this current abstract combines the key points of both articles. As such, this abstract may appear disjointed in places. We hope that our research will contribute meaningfully to the ongoing discussion of traffic modeling and universal diffusion equations. This research focuses on deciphering handwritten mathematical expressions through analysis of sensor-based gesture data. The study examines the feasibility of detecting mathematical symbols during the writing process. A novel approach to identifying handwritten symbols is presented, differentiated from prior works by its non-sequential nature and reliance on gesture data. A statistical symbol identification method is developed and assessed using a collected dataset of handwritten mathematical expressions. The study evaluates two driving signals, sensor force and height, and their combination, using classification metrics on symbol height alone as a baseline. The findings reveal that using both force and height signals in a probability-based classification enhances offline handwriting recognition performance, surpassing that of height alone by 35%, with significant improvements in precision, recall, F1 score, and accuracy. The achieved accuracy is 92%, establishing a basis for real-time handwritten mathematical expression recognition while being susceptible to changes in writing technique. The study opens avenues for further exploration into real-time handwritten mathematical notation recognition. A dataset known as the HME-DTS dataset is also presented, comprising force, height, and width data of handwritten mathematical expressions for standardization and cross-validation purposes. This study presents an innovative approach for synthesizing speech of varied lengths using a non-statistical method, building upon a prior success with a statistical approach. We develop a neural network-based model, comprising a sequence generator and a median driver, to create synthetic speech with specified utterance lengths. The sequence generator produces speech given a target length, while the median driver selects the most appropriate sequence through a dynamic filtering process guided by utterance lengths. The model is trained using a dataset with lengths ranging from 1 to 20 phonemes. We evaluate the effectiveness of our model in producing synthetic speech with specified lengths and examine its ability to create speech with lengths outside its training range. Furthermore, we analyze the features of its filter model and demonstrate its capability to differentiate between synthetic and genuine speech, while also analyzing its performance in predicting word-level timing information. We compare our model's performance to a prior approach and demonstrate its superiority in producing speech with specified lengths. Additionally, we showcase the effectiveness of our model in creating human-like spoken sentences with specified lengths. We anticipate that this novel approach will contribute to the field of spoken language synthesis. The source code for this model is available at https://github.com/vixxxr1/MedianDrivenSLS.

The software utilizes spatial presence data to predict the probability of species occurrence within a specified area. One of the most distant and powerful cosmic events, type Ia supernovae, drove the discovery of the universe's cosmological scale. Paradoxically, their limited observable quantity hinders our comprehension of their explosion mechanics. Capturing the intricate patterns within their light spectra, which reflects their changing physical conditions as they explode, holds significant value. This research introduces a pioneering stochastic neural network, known as the stochastic autoencoder, tailored to model the variation in type Ia supernovae spectra over time. By treating the spectra as non-interdependent samples, we've developed a novel autoencoder framework, demonstrated here using four epochs of spectra for 29 SN Ia with velocity $4500\rm{km/s}$ as our initial test case. Following training, our generated sequences maintain a low error margin compared to actual measurements. By assessing the reconstructed spectra at untrained time points, we've substantiated the time sequence nature of SN Ia evolution. Additionally, our results suggest the utilization of higher velocity vectors may enhance radiation phase predictions. Our findings indicate the stochastic autoencoder holds promise in furthering supernovae research, offering a potential application for other sequence-based astrophysical data. The project's code is accessible at https://github.com/Chen-Wei-China/SNIA_SAE.ToF.

A massive gravitational lensing by a nearby galaxy distorts and amplifies the light from a distant, star-forming galaxy at a redshift of 2.09, allowing us to observe previously unseen neutral outflows from the galaxy. However, most of the outflows are slow-moving and confined to the galaxy's surrounding areas. Our observations suggest that high-speed outflows are less common than thought, and that they play a lesser role in regulating star formation overall. (Abridged from the Introduction.)

This research investigates whether novel investment approaches negatively impact existing strategies from an economic perspective. We conduct a comprehensive literature review and create our own open-access model to address this question, as previous studies often fail to provide clear answers. Our review reveals that, despite existing research, there is a lack of rigorous economic analysis under uncertainty. To fill this knowledge gap, we develop a simple open-economy model with diverse financial systems, where agents utilize an innovative investment method based on rules similar to those applied in real-world scenarios. Our results indicate that when agents switch to the new method, it is unlikely to cause widespread harm to existing strategies in the current market setup. However, our findings also point to potential harm for some ESG strategies that heavily rely on credit ratings. To further explore the potential impact of these new methods on specific investment product sales, we refine our model using data from the US market and simulate two different scenarios. Our simulations suggest that if most agents adopt the new method, it could lead to a decline in sales of some existing products in the US market. Overall, our research supports the view that these new methods can coexist with existing strategies, as observed in practice. However, we also identify areas for further research to address the remaining uncertainties surrounding these new methods. Modern network defense systems rely heavily on adaptive identification protocols to effectively protect against cyber threats.  Both commercial and open source software vendors utilize advanced protocol analysis to accurately recognize and authorize network traffic.  Vendors' reliance on adaptive identification methods, such as deep packet inspection, to detect and block malicious traffic has become widespread.  Although commercial vendors' techniques are well documented, the methods used by open source vendors remain largely obscure.  Recent advances in machine learning and artificial intelligence technologies have significantly impacted the development of network defense systems, making previously inaccessible techniques, such as adaptive protocol identification, readily available to developers.  The open source community's use of adaptive identification protocols poses significant research questions, and, unfortunately, this research formalizes a previously unrecognized vulnerability, referred to as Assault on Adaptive Protocol Identification (AAPI).  The AAPI vulnerability reveals that identifying the identification protocol used by adaptive networks is a solvable problem, and multiple open source vendors' identification protocols can be easily determined through analysis of network traffic.  The AAPI vulnerability further highlights that identifying certain adaptive networks requires as little as a single packet for classification, and, in cases of other adaptive networks, sending tailored traffic is sufficient to classify them.  The AAPI vulnerability demonstrates that, in contrast to commercial vendors' claims, identifying adaptive networks is a feasible task, and provides evidence that a majority of open source vendors' use adaptive identification protocols.  The AAPI vulnerability serves as a warning, advising vendors to reevaluate their security strategies, and serves as a challenge, urging the development of new network defense techniques.  The AAPI vulnerability was formally described in a research paper, and is being released under a non-disclosure agreement as to the actual names of the vendors involved.  The research paper outlines detailed analysis of both commercial and open source vendors' use of adaptive identification protocols, and includes a comprehensive comparison of adaptive networks' implementation methods.  The research paper further provides a thorough examination of the technical aspects behind the AAPI vulnerability, and includes practical examples of exploited vulnerabilities.  The research paper concludes by outlining the practical security implications of the AAPI vulnerability, and includes a call to action, urging the development of new network defense techniques.  The research paper includes knowledge updates, covering the disclosure of the AAPI vulnerability to vendors, and the development of patches to address the vulnerability.  The research paper is currently being considered for publication in multiple prominent academic journals. Bloom filters provide efficient, memory-based approximations for membership testing. Despite their benefits, they may generate false positives, and a result called false positives rate (FPR) increases significantly as memory usage decreases. To address these limitations, alternative data structures, such as cuckoo filters, hash-train Bloom filters, and simple linear hash, have been proposed. These data structures share the goal of reducing memory usage while minimizing false positives. A recent development, Xor Filter Minwise (XFM), has demonstrated better results than existing solutions. Research reveals that implementing FPR as a separate step, Xor Filter Minwise, outperforms the current best approaches both in terms of compression ratio and processing speed. To further optimize XFM, two new algorithms were introduced: one utilizing Python's built-in bitvector, and another leveraging the hardware capabilities of 64-bit integers for bit manipulation, both resulting in substantial improvements. In particular, the new algorithms decreased the required memory for a given FPR by up to 20 and increased processing speed by as much as 30 compared to XFM. Our research also discovered that the optimized XFM algorithms outperform industry-standard solutions, such as HyperLoglog and Count-Min Sketch, and also outperform Bloom and Mod Count-Min filters. Finally, we introduced a set of flexible tools, allowing for the automatic testing and comparison of different algorithm configurations, and demonstrated the feasibility of using these tools to build a practical, memory-efficient membership tester. The research also includes the public availability of the code, which has been used in our experiments, and an accompanying document, which describes our approach in greater detail. The results of our research validate the hypothesis that it is possible to create an algorithm capable of processing arbitrary data streams at high speeds while also achieving a desirable compression ratio. Furthermore, we were able to design and implement such an algorithm, and also showed that under specific constraints, it is not possible to create any algorithm satisfying both the requirements. Our research also identified key performance metrics influencing the practical feasibility of membership testing at high speeds while also achieving a desirable compression ratio. Additionally, we designed and implemented a memory-efficient membership tester capable of processing arbitrary data streams. The research also validated the feasibility of using a 64-bit integer to represent bits, and also identified the lack of 64-bit integers as a substantial limitation of previous algorithms. Furthermore, we were able to design and implement new algorithms using both Python's built-in bitvector and 64-bit integers, resulting in substantial improvements in both processing speed and compression ratio.

The first explores the contributions of Aleksandr Danilovich Aleksandrov, while the second delves into the achievements of Mikhail Yakovlevich Linberg.  Each segment includes a detailed overview of the mentioned mathematicians' lives and significant works, complemented by additional information on other notable researchers from the same academic lineage. This paper presents a novel approach to derive trends from sequence of events in a dynamic market setting, focusing on the relationship between future movements and past sales. Our research reveals that past sales data alone are insufficient to forecast the future market direction with certainty. Nevertheless, when analyzed in conjunction with historical price changes, trends can be accurately predicted. We introduce two new trend analysis metrics: the Share Price Index (SPI) and the Relative Share Volatility Index (RSVI), both of which exhibit remarkable similarity to established stock market analysis tools, the Relative Strength Index (RSI) and the Bollinger Band. Our findings demonstrate that the SPI and RSVI indices predict future price changes with accuracy, outperforming the existing RSI and Bollinger Band in certain scenarios. These trends can also be utilized to detect market volatility and optimize trading decisions. Furthermore, our analysis of the distribution of price changes and the relationship between past price changes and future sales reveals valuable insights for future research. Our methodology is comprised of four distinct phases: (i) past sales analysis, (ii) trend validation using price changes, (iii) development of new trend metrics, and (iv) trend testing and optimization. This multi-faceted approach is unprecedented in current literature and provides a comprehensive framework for trend analysis in a dynamic market environment influenced by future events. Our sources include real-time market feeds, known as Time, Execution Cost, Shares Sold (TICS) sequences, and statistical software for data analysis. Our experiments are conducted across five distinct currency pairs: EUR/USD, GBP/USD, USD/CHF, USD/JPY, and USD/CAD, all of which exhibit different price change patterns. Our research lays the groundwork for future studies on market trend analysis utilizing TICS data, including combining this data with existing price changes for enhanced trend detection and analysis. Additionally, our work can be further optimized by incorporating other data, such as technical indicators, and investigating the feasibility of forecasting the share quantity based on past sales. These additional layers of research will enhance our current approach and contribute to the vast literature on market trend analysis. Our source code is available for public use at a designated link. This methodology yields notable improvements, with success rates rising from 18% to 90% on our test platform. Our experiments demonstrate that this method surpasses current state-of-the-art deepfake detectors. Our solution also showcases exceptional performance in real-world scenarios, retrieving over 90% of strong deepfakes and fake objects in movie datasets. The presence of a liquid envelope, consisting of a water layer and a NH3-H2O layer, plays a crucial role in determining the internal structure of small, temperate exoplanets like Kepler-10 and LHS 1140. As these planets orbit their stars, the liquid components within them can lead to distinctive mass movements that, in turn, affect the size of the solid core and the outer radius of the planet. In order to identify these mass movements, we propose to analyze the size changes of the planet's shadow during a full transit, rather than focusing solely on the overall radius of the planet as observed from the star's side.

Key factors that can reveal the internal liquid components of these planets include 1) the size and distribution of the solid core, which affects the size of the shadow, 2) the amount and location of the liquid components, which can cause pressure-induced density changes, and 3) the composition of the atmosphere, which can also impact the shadow's dimensions. By using realistic numerical models based on the properties of the solubility balances and gas thermodynamics, we can identify the characteristics that can reveal the presence of the internal liquid components of these planets.

Our results from the planet Kepler-10 show that the size of the shadow changes by as little as 0.0000006 in radius if only considering the solid core's size, but this value increases to as much as 0.00014 if also considering the characteristics of the liquid components. Similarly, our results from the planet LHS 1140 demonstrate that the size of the shadow changes by as little as 0.0000003 in radius if only considering the solid core's size, but this value increases to as much as 0.00006 in radius if also considering the characteristics of the liquid components. These large variations in radius can potentially be identified during a full transit, and we plan to analyze this in a future paper. A novel self-organizing spiking neural network architecture is introduced in this study, which enables the learning of diverse visual patterns using biological realistic parameters. The network's neurons adhere to a strict biological model of spike dynamics, and its connectivity is characterized by random excitatory and inhibitory relationships between neurons. Furthermore, the network incorporates a novel mechanism for regulating spike timing accuracy. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate that our spiking neural network is capable of self-organizing and mapping input patterns onto stable, long-term configurations of neuronal firing patterns. The effects of key network parameters, such as size and spike dynamics, are also examined in detail. This study investigates the solvability of restricted Markov decision processes (RMDPs) under various conditions. An RMDP is a multi-objective MDP with limited control options for state transitions. We demonstrate that solving average-reward RMDPs with state-action constraints is computationally infeasible, even in finite RMDPs. However, we also develop an algorithm to solve time-discounted RMDPs with state-action constraints, given that the constraints have a finite number of specifications and the optimal value of these constraints has a finite impedance gap. The proposed algorithm utilizes the primary-dual method, taking the optimal value of the constraints as a dual variable to determine the optimal policy in the primal problem. The complexity of this algorithm is directly proportional to the number of state-action pairs and the square of the number of specifications. Furthermore, we present a series of examples to illustrate the applicability and feasibility of our algorithm in real-world scenarios. Additionally, we discuss the extension of our results to more complex scenarios such as probabilistic target sequences and multiple objective functions. Recent advancements in Reinforcement Learning technologies drive towards making robots autonomous in a variety of settings. Our research focuses on improving the robustness and accountableness of Reinforcement Learning, particularly in Actor-Critic methods, by leveraging Hamiltonian Monte Carlo techniques. This combination yields an adaptable policy learning algorithm that can be effectively utilized in both Markov Decision Processes and continuous action spaces. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo's simulated dynamics facilitate the exploration of action spaces with the goal of accurately estimating the posterior distribution of rewards and actions. Our novel approach replaces traditional random exploratory actions in Actor-Critic methods with informed exploratory actions, thus enabling more efficient use of data. Moreover, by sampling from a common distribution, simultaneous learning of multiple policies becomes feasible, along with a significant reduction in learning time. Comprehensive simulations in diverse environments demonstrate the merits of our approach, revealing consistent performance enhancements over existing Reinforcement Learning methods. The Twin Prime Hypothesis asserts that there is no pair of consecutive prime numbers with a difference of more than $2$. We will demonstrate that this hypothesis is true, yet our approach lacks a conventional proof as it relies on an unproven premise regarding the nature of prime numbers. 

Let's start by defining a prime number as a prime number n, with the property that there are no other prime numbers between the numbers (n-2) and (n-1). We will also define a prime pair as a pair of consecutive prime numbers. We are interested in showing that there are no prime pairs with a difference of more than 2.

Now, consider all prime numbers up to a specific number N, which can be thought of as a very large number. We will denote the largest prime pair up to N as P. In this scenario, we want to show that P is a twin prime, which means that the difference between the two primes is either 0 or 1.

Our approach to this problem involves dividing all prime numbers up to N into sets of prime pairs and lone prime numbers. Since the total count of prime numbers up to N is equal to the sum of all prime pairs up to P, plus the count of lone prime numbers up to N, where each prime pair contributes a count of 2 and each lone prime contributes a count of 1, we can express this relationship mathematically as:

$2f(N) + g(N) = \pi(N)$

Where $\pi(N)$ represents the total count of prime numbers upo N, $f(N)$ represents the total count of prime pairs up to N, and $g(N)$ represents the total count of lone prime numbers up to N.

This paper presents a cutting-edge navigation system for autonomous ground robots, which addresses the limitations of low-cost sensors in challenging environments with heavy interference from weather conditions and diverse terrain. By integrating a ultrasonic sensor with a opticalENC28J60-based Ethernet interface, the proposed system achieves real-time sonar calibration. This is crucial in accurately determining the robot's position, as opticalENC28J60 is prone to interference from digital signals. To rectify this issue, a novel method utilizing Ethernet traffic analysis and a parallel data transfer technique has been developed. Furthermore, a navigation algorithm utilizing the modified Heath-Jardine-Stein error measure has been designed to optimize sensor calibration. Simulation and real-world testing have shown significant improvements in navigation accuracy with the integrated sonar system. Key findings include a 30% reduction in localisation error and 50% reduction in divergence. Moreover, the integrated sonar system has yielded a 90% reduction in navigation error compared to a single sonar sensor. All software and hardware components are open-source and available for public access. This includes the navigation controller software, sonar calibration library, and custom-designed Ethernet-based sonar sensor module. This research aims to promote affordable and accessible autonomous navigation technology. Details of the project, including the repository, can be found at https://github.com/AbdullahAbdullah7/Real-Time-Sonar-Calibration. Our study reveals that tori prevail in this context, extending a prior theorem by Polya for the sole case of the integers. Additionally, our work restricts the diversity of groups meeting this criterion by applying the minimal counterobject concept. It's worth noting that examining tori prevalence in group products is a longstanding, unsolved problem dating back to the 1950s. Our computation of tori prevalence in products of two finite groups, coupled with a proffered conjecture on the prevalence in products of three finite groups, jointly contribute new insights to this longstanding, unsolved problem. Moreover, our work also establishes a prevalence limit for groups that, when expressed as products of their torsion and torsion-free parts, possess a torsion part consisting of only one element. Our analysis employs the fundamental proffered conjecture on the prevalence in products of three finite groups, dubbed the CCC. Our study also explores a generalized version of the CCC for both finite and compact groups, dubbed the multi-CCC. A key aspect of our work involves demonstrating that the multi-CCC holds true for both amenable and compact groups. Analyzing molecular profiles using high-dimensional data with a large number of variables and limited sample size presents significant challenges, primarily due to the uncertainty and variability associated with such data. In high-dimensional data sets, popular distance metrics may not effectively capture relationships among samples, especially when variables exhibit non-linear correlations. This study compares the performance of six high-dimensional data clustering methods, including a novel approach, in classifying samples based on their molecular characteristics. These methods utilize a new metric called the Proportion-weighted Reverse Kernel distance, in conjunction with proportion existence-based data transforms, to emphasize variable-to-sample interactions and minimize noise in the data. Comprehensive evaluations through multiple random trials revealed that the Proportion-weighted Reverse Kernel distance performed better than other methods in predicting known sample groups. Notably, an intrinsic evaluation without pre-selecting variables identified sample groups that matched existing knowledge of tumor subtypes, revealing the presence of distinct subtypes of acute myeloid leukemia, such as M2-like subtypes. These findings were further validated using independent data from The Cancer Genome Atlas. Additional analyses demonstrated that the Proportion-weighted Reverse Kernel distance could accurately predict known molecular profiles, identify subtype-specific patterns, and make predictions for individual patient samples, thus showing great promise in the analysis and interpretation of high-dimensional molecular data. Our approach to detecting offensive tweets combines BERT and Support Vector Machines. Since the task involved two subtasks with different evaluation criteria, our strategy varied accordingly. For subtask A, which focused on binary classification with an information retrieval metric, our model utilized pre-trained BERT embeddings combined with static word embeddings, static BERT-based phrases, and their corresponding centroids, all of which were trained using SVM classifiers. Our approach proved successful, achieving a macro F1 score of 0.9426 in the development set and 0.8831 in the test set. In subtask B, which required multi-class classification with a macro F1 metric, our model built upon the foundation established in subtask A. Specifically, we applied a clustering-based classifier to determine offensiveness towards specific groups. Our cumulative results revealed high macro F1 scores of 0.9235 in the development set and 0.8491 in the test set for three categories: social media users, professionals, and organizations. Nevertheless, we encountered challenges in capturing the nuanced offensiveness towards specific groups, particularly in subtask B, where our model struggled to differentiate between the three categories. Our code and data are available for public access at https://github.com/UM-IU-LING/UM_IU_LING_SemEval-2019_C6.

Computed Tomography (CT) is a fundamental imaging technique used across multiple fields to derive detailed insights into various types of subjects and objects. Since X-rays interact differently with diverse materials, CT data inherently includes information on the density and atomic number of subjects. Ideally, reconstructing CT images would involve simultaneously considering X-ray interaction and energy loss as well as multiple energy sources, yet current techniques typically rely on simplified models and single-energy scans. Motivated by advancements in sensor technology allowing for simultaneous multi-spectral measurements, this research develops a unified variational framework that accounts for non-trivial energy loss and multi-energy data. To withstand harsh environmental conditions, this model also includes a sensor noise reduction component and a component simulating realistic tissue behavior. We demonstrate effective image reconstruction capabilities using the proposed framework, successfully processing synthetic and real-world scanning data. Furthermore, our results showcase that using multi-energy data can yield more accurate density and material composition images compared to single-energy data. To validate the feasibility of sensor noise reduction, we demonstrate enhanced image quality with reduced noise when applying our approach. Lastly, our model's ability to simulate realistic tissue behavior is substantiated by comparing our reconstructed images with official RadData datasets. Additionally, we provide open-source code and guidance on replicating our research at the provided URL. We expect our work to contribute positively to the ongoing discussion on propagating CT's inherent multi-energy capabilities. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a complex challenge, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and significant variability in handwriting styles across different regions. To overcome this problem, we focus on developing a method that generates large amounts of high-quality synthetic data from a limited number of perfect transcripts and corresponding image segments. Since CDHTR requires taking both text and image into account during training, we propose using a normalizing transformation to eliminate the influence of text content and instead leverage image features and a pre-existing text dataset to create synthetic data. To validate our approach, we conducted experiments on three handwritten languages and compared its effectiveness against two alternative methods one of which involves generating random characters. While the results indicate that our approach outperforms the others, we observed that the success of this strategy heavily depends on the quality of the used image features. To address this issue, we further developed a supplementary strategy called Single-shot Compositional Data Creation (SSCDC) which utilizes a fully convolutional auto-encoder to create synthetic data from single instances of handwritten characters, thereby producing more realistic results. Through a series of ablation studies, we analyzed SSDC's potential to improve models trained on HTR datasets. The source code for our approach is available at https://github.com/asharaki/HTR_Composition.

To address the challenge of incorporating large-scale linear system solving into ab initio nuclear physics computations, researchers are adapting various scalable linear solver algorithms originally developed for high-performance computational simulations. Specifically, the authors have successfully merged the ab initio no-core lattice simulation code with a modern linear solver algorithm from the High Performance Computing library, PETSc. This new combination enables the computation of heavy nuclear ground states by utilizing finite-dimensional approximations of many-body lattice determinants. Detailed analysis demonstrates that the merged code maintains the accuracy of the lattice simulation, while efficiently utilizing parallel computing resources to tackle complex nuclear physics problems. As a proof of concept, the authors successfully calculated the ground state wavefunctions of 42-He, 42-Li, 50-Ne, and 82-Si isotopes. Future directions for development and applying this code are also discussed. Furthermore, the authors have open-sourced the code and research methodology, making it available at https://git.uq.edu.au/viewgit.php/phys-phy0800 NC Lancaster/tree/main/ Petroc public. This research project focuses on a specific type of tube called a straw conduit, used in certain industrial applications, and investigates how it reacts to external pressure and temperature variations. To achieve this, the project applies finite element methods to analyze and model the structural behavior of the straw conduit under different conditions. Utilizing a strain-driven approach based on the generalized strain energy method, the researchers modeled and simulated various stress scenarios. The results show that when subjected to uniform internal pressure, the straw conduit experiences significant axial deformation, and upon warming, it contracts in both axial and radial directions. Furthermore, the researchers identified the regions most susceptible to failure and demonstrated the capability of these structures to function within a stable, continuous strain range. Knowledge gained from these studies can be instrumental in predicting and managing strain in similar structural components. Based on the findings, the researchers recommend implementing cooling systems to prevent strain-related damage and ensure the structural integrity of these conduits. Although this research specifically utilizes data from a prototype cone valve, the theoretical framework has broad applications that can be extended to other types of straw conduits. In fact, similar analysis can be applied to design and evaluate valves, such as the ConValValve, used in high-energy particle colliders, and other types of industrial and industrial-like applications. Given its generalizability, the findings of this study can be relevant to a range of valving technologies. To expand the scope of this research, the researchers suggest modeling and simulating other types of valves, such as the types currently employed at the Large Hadron Collider, and analyzing their behavior under various conditions to gain a deeper understanding of their structural behavior and potential failures. This could ultimately lead to the development of predictive models that can be used to optimize the design and performance of these structures. In particular, the researchers propose simulating the behavior of valves under extreme operating conditions to uncover potential failures and develop strategies for mitigating them. This could involve modeling scenarios such as rapid changes in temperature, pressure, and other factors that may not have been accounted for in the design of these structures. In deep network classification, adopting a Bayesian approach helps to quantify uncertainty but identifying reliable confidence levels remains an area of concern. This study investigates "sturdiness assurances" - confidence levels that can be relied upon - in Credal Bayesian Networks. Our approach involves comparing and contrasting traditional sturdiness definitions with an adapted version, which involves analyzing the reliability of posterior credibility sets within the context of probabilistic circuits. Inconsistent sturdiness definitions lead to imprecise and potentially misleading results, but our proposed notion of sturdiness assures precision by verifying the sturdiness definition's robustness against variations in constraint tightening or loosening in the probabilistic circuit. Our research demonstrates that precise sturdiness assurances can be achieved, but we also uncover cases where sturdiness assurances cannot be guaranteed. To resolve uncertainty, we develop an iterative procedure, known as Sturdiness Assurance Finder, which identifies sturdiness assurances in Credal Bayesian Networks through the iterative refinement of credibility sets in the probabilistic circuit. In supersolid phases featuring both liquid-like and solid-like movements, a typical prediction is that sound waves propagating through the liquid-like component are accompanied by density fluctuations both within the solid and liquid structures.  However, in the event that these density fluctuations occur at the same rate as the sound waves, it could become difficult to distinguish the impact of the sound waves on the density fluctuations from their typical collective modes.  This study takes into account both the long-wavelength and long-time limits of the low-momentum sound modes of a specific model for ultracold bosonic stars that form in the presence of magnetic field fluctuations.  It finds that, although the density fluctuations are generally smaller than the sound waves, their impact can still be significant at longer times.  As a result, the observation of these density fluctuations may become complicated by their similarity to collective modes that are already well understood.  Additionally, the investigation reveals that the frequency at which the density fluctuations occur is not affected by the applied magnetic field.  By contrast, the lifetime of these fluctuations is found to increase with the strength of the magnetic field.  It is also determined that the conditions necessary to observe both the sound waves and the density fluctuations at the same time may be more challenging to satisfy than previously thought.  Finally, the study provides an estimation of the intensity of the density fluctuations in relation to the sound waves, suggesting that the density fluctuations are significantly less intense than the sound waves.  It is proposed that experimental investigations be conducted using smaller, isolated droplets of the supersolid.  It is also suggested that other models for supersolid phases may produce different results than the model investigated in this study.  Consequently, further theoretical research is required to confirm whether the density fluctuations can survive as long as the sound waves. The Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) at the heart of the Milky Way is both dynamically important and fascinating due to its potential star formation, but the actual mass distribution within this region remains unclear. By using data from the Fragmentation Survey of Transient Massive Star Formation, we created a visual representation of the mass arrangement in the CMZ by comparing the mass of molecular cloud substructures in a two-dimensional grid. This approach allowed us to identify areas with high molecular mass and to establish a relationship between those masses and the overall cloud mass. As a result, we found that the mass distribution in the CMZ is not random, as regions with high molecular mass tend to be located in a spiral pattern, which suggests a need for further study on how the arrangement of the CMZ's molecular clouds affects their formation of stars. Additionally, we found that the mass arrangement in the CMZ changes over time, as observed in the Perseus and 30 Doradus molecular clouds. Further studies are needed to understand the underlying physical mechanisms that govern the formation and evolution of the CMZ's molecular clouds. Measurements of x-ray absorption near edge spectra reveal the rapid changes that occur within molecular systems when they are near an intense x-ray pulse. The significant disparity in x-rays and electrons leads to a need for a simplified framework to understand this phenomenon. The proposed rate framework distinguishes between electron groups with varying response times, allowing for first-order decay of selected groups and others to be described through relaxation times. The number of electron groups needed for an accurate description is determined by the highest frequency component within the x-ray pulse. The rate framework can capture density-dependent phenomena observed in experiments and is consistent with quantum theory, making it a valuable tool for explaining observed trends and predicting future measurements. The approach can also be extended to describe changes in other molecular properties during an x-ray pulse. Additionally, the concept of electron groups can be used for modeling valence excitation and subsequent changes in the electronic structure of molecules. Further developments of the idea could lead to a fundamental understanding of how matter responds to intense pulses of light and how their interactions affect molecular phenomena. The description of electronic excitation and relaxation, based on the rate framework and requiring only basic parameters, enables the calculation of time-resolved x-ray absorption spectra, providing a straightforward method to compute these spectra and simulate measured data as shown in several cases, including experiments involving ions, molecules, and metal-organic frameworks. Most importantly, the rate framework offers an actionable strategy to analyze measured data and extract crucial information about the excited states of investigated systems, demonstrating this approach for certain examples. In order to make the calculation of time-resolved x-ray absorption spectra more efficient, the rate framework can be adapted into a semi-empirical form that focuses on the most critical electronic processes, resulting in only a few essential parameters that need to be optimized for an excellent fit of measured spectra. The semi-empirical version of the rate framework not only facilitates the reproduction and simulation of existing measurement data, but it also allows for precise predictions of time-resolved x-ray absorption spectra, based on solely the structural knowledge of the sample under investigation. Moreover, this version can provide valuable insights into the dynamics of molecules and their response to an intense x-ray pulse. A comparison between calculated and measured spectra reveals very satisfactory results, underscoring the effectiveness and simplicity of the rate framework to describe molecular phenomena. We introduce a distorted resolvent method to build Nash equilibria for a wide range of econometric models, encompassing single and multi-product industries, as well as transport costs. This novel approach deforms the resolvent operator to facilitate analytical and numerical solutions. Both analytical and numerical examples are provided to illustrate the method's effectiveness, revealing its advantages in terms of computational efficiency and ease of implementation. Additionally, we examine the distoration of operators and their implications for Nash equilibrium construction. Our findings indicate that distoration can enhance computational convergence and even permit the construction of Nash equilibria in models previously intractable with standard methods. Like many operator distortions, the resolvent distortion we propose has a straightforward economic interpretation, reflecting adjustments made to firms' marginal costs to ensure the existence of a Nash equilibrium. In this spirit, we explore a broader class of resolvent distorsions, encompassing both our previous example and an alternative scenario where firms' price adjustments are distorted. Both of these alternative distorsions can be applied to models of competitive equilibrium. Our analysis provides a unified framework for understanding the role of distorsions in Nash equilibrium and competitive equilibrium models. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the distorted resolvent method offers a versatile tool for tackling a diverse array of economic equilibrium problems. A novel method called U reversible Steganography is proposed as an improvement over existing approaches like least significant bit steganography. Since existing methods are susceptible to detection, we developed a framework for steganography that maintains the integrity of the cover file and prevents exposure. The key innovation of our method involves redefining the steganography problem as an inference task within a Bayesian neural network context. By formulating the problem in such a way, we can quantify the uncertainty associated with each message bit and identify the specific network inputs that can help retrieve hidden messages. Furthermore, we developed a metric called $\mathcal{U}$ to assess the level of uncertainty associated with each message bit, and demonstrated the efficacy of our method by showing that it surpasses state-of-the-art methods in terms of payload capacity, cover file size, and Q-factor. The code for our approach can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/AbhayKumar-BNN-US. Experimental results indicate that the steganographic data survives even the most stringent conditions imposed by the Q-factor, and can be successfully retrieved with high accuracy from nosy covers even when the level of uncertainty associated with each message bit is as low as 0.10. In particular, we achieved payload capacities of approximately $4.82k$, $4.80k$, and $4.77k$ bits for cover files of size 256k, demonstrating the versatility of our approach. A detailed analysis of our method, along with its many potential applications and extensions, is included in this manuscript. Furthermore, we envisioned two possible scenarios for which our method may be a suitable candidate: (i) maintaining confidentiality of communication in a quantum environment, and (ii) protecting sensitive information from being exposed in a scenario where the information sender and receiver share the same platform. These scenarios, along with several other potential use-cases, are discussed in the conclusion section. Additionally, we presented an alternative method called US based on the hidden activation steeganography technique, which can be easily integrated into existing neural networks without requiring any additional training. We've identified two types of shadow matter candidates in frameworks featuring three Higgs doublets with symmetry group S_3. These candidates, denoted as P and Q, are naturally weakly-interacting with particles other than the Higgs bosons. However, they strongly couple with at least one type of Higgs boson in a manner that mirrors the relationship between standard matter and shadow matter. In our analysis, we've selected scenarios where P and Q's mass spectra consist of two nearly degenerate masses and a heavier mass. By assuming that radiative decays are suppressed, we've established parameters for P and Q's masses that are in line with constraints from particle-phyysics observations. We demonstrate that circular likelihoods are a unique combination of positive definite matrices and propose an alternative representation for circular likelihoods using graph theory. We then develop an algorithm to sample from the posterior distribution of a nontransitive model, specifically designed for comparative data. Our approach is illustrated with an example of bird evolutionary relationships. We further examine the relationship between circular and nontransitive likelihoods and prove a strict inequality holds in general, although an equalit y condition is satisfied when the likelihood matrix is symmetric. We provide an example of a nontransitive relationship that satisfies this symmetry condition. Finally, we introduce a new metric for comparing the strength of circular and nontransitive relationships. This metric is utilized to analyze bird evolutionary relationships and show that some relationships exhibiting high degrees of nontransitivity may also exhibit strong circular patterns. On the other hand, we demonstrate that transitive relationships are characterized by a lack of nontransitive and circular features. Our work expands the understanding of statistical models through the exploration of relational invariants. It further highlights that strong transitivity does not necessarily imply a lack of nontransitive and circular relationships, but demonstrates that nontransitive and circular relationships are inherent characteristics of transitive ones. Current deep reinforcement learning training methods often utilize model-based approaches, where a reward prediction model is trained alongside policy networks. However, when the reward model is not compatible with the new configuration, it becomes challenging for the trainer to adapt to the new environment. This study introduces a method to mitigate this issue by training a reward model that can easily adjust to changes, alongside separate, modularized policy networks for distinct tasks. The evaluation of this approach in multiple domains, including power management and navigation, demonstrates significant benefits in handling unexpected system changes during multi-task reinforcement learning training. The findings indicate that training separate policy networks for each task, with a shared reward model, not only maintains performance under normal and altered conditions, but also enhances overall training efficiency. The empirical results show a notable gain in processing speed, with a processing speed up of 3.91 times for task adaptation under changed environments, and a 2.97 times processing speed up for simultaneous training of multiple tasks. Initially, the system's behavior is orderly, with periodic oscillations; however, as it reaches a critical energy threshold, it gives way to a complex, disordered state. To quantify this transformation, we define and count two sets relevant to the Hénon-Heiles system: the sets of trajectories following it leads to quasi-periodic and chaotic trajectories. This note expands upon a hypothesis initially proposed in ref. \[1\], suggesting that scalar fields with profound histories may persist for extended periods, potentially invalidating cosmetic scalings in scalar field theories.
We argue that, in contrast to conventional scalar field theories, a scalar field with a prolonged history may give rise to stabilising loops, particularly concerning Higgs inflation and similar scenarios. The implication of this idea for future high-energy collider experiments is that the desired sensitivity to new scalar bosons may necessitate more stringent demands on precision and a broader search spectrum than previously anticipated. We also explore other crucial considerations, including the scalar field's stability during prolonged existence and the potential for inflation to either $k$-inflation or hilltop scenarios. Additionally, we outline a hypothetical case in which extra dimensions could give rise to prolonged scalar phenomena at the LHC. We hope that this notice will inspire a fresh perspective on scalar physics and future high-energy collider research. 
Keywords: prolonged scalar, Higgs inflation, $k$-inflation, hilltop inflation, collider physics, extra dimensions.

This paper presents a generative framework called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, based on an autoregressive method, to generate raw audio signals in real-time. By integrating a pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural network into the WaveNet framework, Quasi-Periodic WaveNet effectively learns complex patterns in long-term audio sequences. Experimental results on the LibriSpeech dataset reveal that Quasi-Periodic WaveNet outperforms WaveNet in terms of log-loss error, while also achieving faster training and inference times. To optimize performance, a posterior-guided sampling technique was also developed. Additionally, the generated audio data is accessible through a public online demo. Our source code is freely available on GitHub at https://github.com/yindengy/Quasi-Periodic-Wavenet.

To further investigate this connection, the theorem of equivalence between unitary shadows and functors from the category of finite sets to bicategories is demonstrated. Additionally, the category of connections on a bicategory, a concept developed by Markings theory, is defined and its connection to shadows, specifically the concept of unitary shadows, is established through the theorem of equivalence between unitary shadows and marks of bicategories. We introduce a new approach to image tone mapping, where multiple images with varied exposure levels are used to derive a universal style that can be applied to new images with different exposures. This is achieved through a two-step process - first, multiple images are used to extract style features through a multi-scale neural network, while a single image is used in a generative model to produce a new image in a different exposure. Our method is based on the idea that similar scenes under different exposures share similar characteristics, and by extracting style features from a set of images, we can apply them to new images to produce a consistent look. Additionally, our method inverts the process to generate new images given a target look. Our method outperforms current methods in a comprehensive dataset and performs well in applications such as global tone mapping and style transfer. Developing autonomous systems for independent decision-making is a major goal.
Traditional methods used for autonomous robot navigation are largely influenced by
supervisory controls, limiting the ability to learn and adapt in a decentralized
environment. 
This paper proposes a new framework based on Profound Active Deduction (PAD), a
general method for autonomous decision-making that can be applied to robot navigation.
By incorporating the robot's environment and available information into its reasoning,
PAD enables the robot to make uninformed decisions, ultimately improving its ability
to navigate unfamiliar areas and reduce dependence on external supervision. 
We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through a practical application to
an autonomous robot navigating a maze. 
MazeWorld, a self-contained environment with dynamic rules, is used to show how
PAD facilitates decentralized decision-making and learning, compared to other popular
autonomous methods. 
MazeWorld and its associated decision-making logic are available online. 
This research validates the potential of PAD as a general method for autonomous decision-making
in a range of scenarios, including (but not limited to) robot navigation. 
MazeWorld will be made available at https://mazznow.github.io/maznow/. 
Please note that this research does NOT involve real robots and is focused solely on theoretical
decision-making.

Using a technique similar to that described in [19], we translate the equations into a framework suitable for proof-based verification. Following this, we apply a series of inductive steps to demonstrate that the helicity functional remains constant. This outcome holds significant importance as the helicity functional serves as a preserved quantity for ideal magnetohydrodynamics, playing a crucial role in its simplified mathematical formulation. By extending this evaluation to the compressible Euler equations, we enable the examination of helicity in a broader context, including scenarios where gases are not ideal. This study reveals that when a strong shock wave collapses, it leads to the formation of a rarefaction wave and ultimately, a series of shock waves and sound waves. For the development and training of computer-aided systems in colorectal polyps diagnosis, high-quality histopathological images are essential. Currently, there are significant limitations in the field due to the lack of large, well-annotated image datasets specifically designed for this purpose. To address this issue, we have created UniToPatho, a comprehensive dataset consisting of 13,421 histological images of colorectal polyps along with detailed pathological markings. Our dataset spans from non-neoplastic to adenomatous polyps and includes three levels of adenoma abnormalities. This resource is groundbreaking, as it is one of the largest of its kind and comprehensive in its coverage of adenoma grades. We are proud to announce that UniToPatho is now available at https://git.io/UniToPatho. Our research aims to showcase the potential of this dataset by introducing three classification tasks and accompanying baselines. We hope that our research will facilitate the advancement of new approaches and methods within the field. We invite other researchers to collaborate with us and contribute to the continuous growth of UniToPatho. 
Details of our collaborations are documented at https://unito-patho.github.io/index.html. 
Our paper has been accepted at the MICCAI 2022 polyp detection challenge.

This study explores the complex historical relationships between mathematics and philosophy during the scientific Renaissance in Italy from the late 16th to the early 17th century. Despite mathematics emerging as the primary language of scientific expression, philosophers continued to prioritize verbal explanations over numerical methods. I examine this dichotomy through a case study of Galileo's conflict with philosopher Cesare Cremonini, who rejected the latter's refusal to utilize mathematics in scientific inquiry, thus failing to appreciate the significant contributions mathematics made to science in this period. Additionally, I analyze how mathematics addressed philosophical concerns in several key texts, including the writings of Bonaventura Cavalieri, Alphonso Antonio, and Vincenzo Viviani. Furthermore, I investigate how mathematics responded to existential and metaphysical inquiries, revealing a notable shift in its relationship with philosophy following the discovery of incommensurability in the 16th century. The fundamental change mathematics underwent during this time not only transformed its operational capabilities, as is widely acknowledged, but also transformed its relationship with philosophy, as mathematics emerged as a distinct, autonomous discipline that could address various philosophical concerns. I started coding in 2015, but my progress stalled until I revived my skills in 2020 by creating Amanuensis, a simple web app that tracks my GitHub repository activity and provides a public history of my progress. By committing to regular code reviews, I revived my skills and maintained a record of my journey as a coder. This system has benefits for not only new but also experienced programmers, offering a way to document their progress and reflect on their past work. Amanuensis is an open-source platform that allows users to connect their GitHub accounts and track their activity across various repositories, displaying a searchable log of events that can be exported as Markdown files or emailed in summary form. I introduce Amanuensis as a tool to support programmers in sustaining their coding skills throughout their careers.
